utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. Good morning, everybody. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I only notice the absence of Mr. Bourgon. The Prosecution composition of the Prosecution team is as yesterday. The witness is already present. Good morning to you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you and good morning to you, Your Honours. Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, yesterday we spoke about the action taken by the 28th Division from the Srebrenica area, and I'm talking about Serbian territory now, but can we just go back briefly to the subject that you discussed with my learned friend Mr. Zivanovic, who was cross-examining you, the shelling of Srebrenica. I asked you about your proofing session yesterday. I asked you about the proofing notes that you received from the OTP as well, and you told me you've never seen those. Let me tell you one thing that I found in those notes, and I'm expecting you to please just confirm whether you shared anything like that with the OTP during your actual proofing or not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours, good morning, everyone. Sorry to intervene so early. I'm don't know whether it's just a translation or transcription issue. I don't think there's any evidence and it's certainly not the case that this witness was furnished with my proofing notes. I just wanted to clarify that before we went any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Then I apologise. It's probably, then, a translation issue. I mean, the witness was very clear that he never received this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then it is definitely, I mean, because that's what the transcript says.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is why -- this is why I would just like to quote this part of the proofing notes to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Colonel, is it clear to you? No one is suggesting that you were handed a copy of the proofing notes, but reference is going to be made to them and you're going to be asked a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Fine, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You see, Colonel, I'm looking at your proofing notes and I found the following sentence. I'll read it back to you. Tell me whether you shared anything like that with the OTP during the proofing? [In English] "The Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina Communication Centre would constitute a legitimate military target." [Interpretation] Therefore, is it your position that the Army's Communication Centre would constitute a legitimate target, which it is therefore legitimate to fire upon?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. If we could just elaborate on this a little, may I ask you this: What about, for example, a building housing the headquarters of a military unit, would that, too, constitute a legitimate military target, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would like to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honours, I have to give a brief explanation regarding this document. We were working very hard on documents regarding this case, and the late - "late" meant last evening - very lately, we discovered one document which we found very significant for this case. I only have it in hard copy, one copy in B/C/S. I already informed my colleague, Mr. Thayer, about this document. We will do our best to provide the Trial Chamber with a -- with translation of this document as soon as practical, but we find it highly important for this case. It's a document dated the 22nd of February, 1995. It is from Srebrenica, and it is basically a list of premises that were used by the 28th Division within Srebrenica and the surrounding villages. It contains something like - I didn't count it - but maybe around 20 places where various portions of 28th Division's headquarters, staff communications centre, and other -- other parts of 28th Division were located within Srebrenica. So I would just like to put it on the ELMO, so I don't know whether the witness can help us much with it. It's in B/C/S, but I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the -- what's the source of this document? Is it a document provided by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We found it on the EDS, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay, that's enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm perfectly aware of the fact that you can't help us much with this document, since we don't have it in a language that you understand. But it is a very important document for our purposes, so I'll be asking you questions about certain details from this document in order to clarify a number of issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Can we just see the lower -- the upper part? Is it possible to have the whole page on the screen? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, Colonel, this document was found within the possession of the OTP. What we see here is the commander of the 28th Division. As far as I can see, it says: "Inspection of the premises used by the Armed Forces of the Republic of B and H, Tuzla Secretariat of Defence," and then at "1" we see the Command of the 8th Operations Group of Srebrenica. Now you, told us already at one point in time the 28th Division had its name changed to "Operations Group 8." Do you remember telling us that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You see what it says here, don't you? The commander or the HQ of OG-8 is at a facility known as "Lovac" in Srebrenica's old town. Are you familiar with that facility, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the name, not maybe the facility you're talking about, but I'm familiar with the name "Lovac."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: At "B" we see that the facility is being used by the Command of OG-8. There's the area mentioned, the surface, and it says it's being used by the Command. Roman numeral II, the 280 1st Light Infantry Brigade of Potocari, the family home owned by Meho Hrvacic at Potocari. That's wait says. I assume you don't know specifically which home this might be, but what this document tells us is that it was used for the purposes of the 280th Brigade. Further, at 2(a), facility, old Territorial Defence staff in Srebrenica. Do you happen to know where that building is located?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know where it's located, unless maybe you give me a specific location; otherwise, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'd love to do that, but frankly I'm not entirely sure myself. Believe me, Colonel, however, we shall find a way of demonstrating that. If we look at the rest of this document, page 1 and page 2, there is a list there of various facilities used either by the Command of OG-8 in Srebrenica or certain brigades that were part of OG-8. There are a total of about 20 facilities, some in Srebrenica and some around Srebrenica in the surrounding villages, apparently being used by various HQs, commands, logistics, sections belonging to the 28th Division or OG-8. In your opinion, sir, and based on everything you've told us so far, would that -- or would those constitute, likewise, legitimate military targets?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it depends on what these facilities were holding. Right now, it's difficult to estimate or even know the kind of equipment which were -- which were there to make it a military target. As far as I know, the building that we were living in, that is, the PTT building, as I said earlier, could have constituted a military target because of its strategic position, and also it's housing the communication equipment. But, really, when you're talking about the whole enclave, then I doubt how it can constitute a military target, and especially when you know for sure it is holding very many civilians and you really do not want the civilians to become a target. For any conventional force, you don't target civilians, you do not, and you avoid hitting areas that have civilians in them. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. Mr. Lazarevic, Mr. Thayer, and Colonel, we allowed the question to go and the witness to start answering it. However, we have moved from what is or what would be a legitimate question to a question which elicits, for all intents and purposes, an opinion by or from the witness on what is strictly legal. We're talking of what constitutes a legitimate target and what doesn't. I mean, I don't think we should ask the witness to give us that information. That is a legal matter that we can deal with at the right moment or when the time comes. So I would suggest that you move either to something else or to refine or limit your question to what would be strictly acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] As always, Your Honour is right and I'll skip to something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, the last thing we talked about yesterday were the attacks launched by the 28th Division, at least based on documents that we saw yesterday. These attacks were carried out against Serb-held territory. You told us that you were familiar with that and everything else that was going on. I have another document from the same set now, the same set as the previous document, I mean. The date is the 23rd of June, 1995. To all practical intents, this is a monthly report by the 28th Division that was forwarded to the 2nd Corps in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in B/C/S, and the ERN number is DA18-2435. Likewise, this is a B/C/S document. Can we just look at the title page, if it could please be placed on the ELMO, and then we shall be focusing on a portion -- a specific portion on page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted you to look at the header of this document, sir. I will translate that for your benefit. It says: "BH Army, Command of the 28th Division, Security section." There is the number and the date, the 23rd of June, 1995. This is a monthly report delivered to the 2nd Corps, which is based in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please move on to page 2 of this document, second paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We see item 3, the situation in the Command and units. I will skip the first sentence, but then it goes on to say: "On the 22nd of June, 1995, DIV Sabotage and Reconnaissance Platoons were dispatched by units to carry out active sabotage in the general Kragljivode area and along the Vlasenica-Han Pijesak Road. Acts of sabotage were launched in order to provide assistance to units of the 1st, 2nd, and other Corps in order to stretch enemy forces." That is the end of the portion that I wanted to show you, sir. What about what I've just told you, does that not, in essence, confirm everything that we've been studying, based on previous documents especially yesterday; namely, the fact that the 28th Division, which obviously was within the Srebrenica enclave, was dispatching its sabotage and reconnaissance platoons in order to carry out acts of sabotage outside the enclave itself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt again, but this matter was dealt with yesterday, I don't know whether by you or Mr. Zivanovic, and the witness explained that insofar as attacks or actions or activities outside the enclave itself, he could tell us nothing. In actual fact, he could tell us barely anything about what was happening inside the enclave, in any case, so I wouldn't like you to ask repetitive questions. Actually, what we have in this document is almost a replication of what we had in another document that we were shown yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] All right, Your Honour, I will then move to another issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, what was your relationship with Dutch-Bat or with UNPROFOR, generally speaking? Did you exchange experiences, information, you and Dutch-Bat, their command, Colonel Karremans, and everybody else there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, correct me if I am wrong, Colonel, but I think you were asked this question yesterday and you explained that you were instructed to exchange views laterally, I remember, and vertically. So if I'm not correct, if it was a different question, I stand to be corrected, but I think it was. I think it was the same question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] The question was slightly different, but this was the foundation of questions for the next line of documents that I would like to show to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There was some exchange of information between you and Dutch-Bat in Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now have 4D00128. 4D00128, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you see the document in front of you. It's in English. You can read that document, but what I'm really interested in is the header. This is a letter written by General Nikolai Cornelis and sent to General Rasim Delic on the 26th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move to page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read the first two paragraphs. They are rather brief. The first one reads: [In English] "I also have to inform you that the commanding officer of Dutch-Bat during the last few weeks for several times had to warn your troops in the enclave to restrain from attacks outside the safe area. "As you will understand, these kinds of attacks cause responses which endanger the safety of the civil population in the safe area and make it very difficult for UNPROFOR to protect the safe area in any an appropriate way." [Interpretation] You see, General Nikolai sent this letter to Rasim Delic, the BH Army general, informing him that UNPROFOR, or rather, the Command of Dutch-Bat in Srebrenica were trying to prevent attacks being carried out from within the enclave against the Serbs. Did you receive this type of information from Dutch-Bat as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, I don't know whether this letter is directed to the CO Dutch-Bat. Secondly, the letter is on an UNPROFOR letterhead, I think - that is what I saw - and is written by two people who are not, I think, working with -- were not working with UNPROFOR. I don't know, but is that what I saw on the first page? I'm not trying to doubt the authenticity of the letter, but what I'm saying is this letter was not addressed to CO Dutch-Bat, and I don't think there's any way I could have come in contact with such a letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That wasn't the question. The question, yes, let's see the first page again. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was just going to ask that perhaps to uncomplicate things, if the witness could just be given a thorough opportunity to read the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's very important for the witness to read the entire document, because the question that Mr. Lazarevic put to him was: "On the basis of what you read in this document, did you ever receive this type of information from Dutch-Bat?" This is what Mr. Lazarevic wants to know from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honours, maybe while we wait for the witness to finish reading this document, maybe I should read for the record the DRN number for the first documents that I used today, because I -- it simply slipped my mind. The document we were dealing with premises used by the 28th Division, dated 22nd of February, 1995, bears number DAA -- DA17-8185.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, you were able to read the whole letter now, and you can see that it was sent by General Nikolai of UNPROFOR to General Rasim Delic, as you can see in the letterhead. You can also see who received it. Therefore, General Nikolai sent this information for which he says he had received from the Dutch-Bat commander. My question is: Did you receive the same information from the Dutch-Bat commander?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not receive any information concerning this, this letter, or any issues therein, only that at least I know there was no fuel. But information coming from Dutch-Bat concerning this, I did not receive.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you another thing concerning this matter. Concerning these events, there was an investigation conducted by Dutch-Bat members. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there's one thing that I may try to clear, in that it's not everything that was going on in Dutch-Bat that I had to know. They did not have to tell me everything, and, in fact, there was no obligation for them to tell me anything. Likewise, even what we heard is not -- was not necessarily to be directed or communicated to them in any way whatsoever, other than where we think there is a mutual interest in some of these issues. The letters, they were being directed to them, and they didn't have to disclose whether the letters had gone to them or even the contents of those letters to any of us. There was no obligation on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that fully. However, there was an order in place -- well, I'm not sure whether it was an order or an instruction for you to cooperate with them, to cooperate with the Dutch-Bat command. Both you and them were members of the UN; therefore, such cooperation would only have been logical. What I find interesting is that these are significant incidents with dozens of killed and wounded on the Serb side, and yet it seems you did not exchange that type of information with Dutch-Bat members. This is what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to have a look at 4D129 in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Again, it is the 26th of June, 1995, and, again, General Nikolai is sending a letter to General Mladic this time. Therefore, there was communication at that level between General Nikolai and General Delic as well as General Mladic. In the first paragraph of the letter, it reads: [In English] "In response to your letter number 06/17-441 of 24 June 1995 with reports on several attacks from the safe area of Srebrenica, I ordered an immediate investigation. That investigation made me recognise that at the times and places mentioned in your letter, combat activities by BiH troops had really occurred." [Interpretation] You can see from the letter that General Nikolai is confirming that those attacks had occurred and that there was an investigation. Do you have an explanation as to why this -- this was not known to you, since you were an UN monitor?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, when you say that these things happened and I did not know, what there is is that when somebody these things are happening at higher levels, the generals' level and all that, sometimes it may not trickle down to us down there. The fact is I was not informed of this kind of investigation. I'm not aware of it; and if the results were made to anybody, or if the investigations were ordered by somebody, somewhere, their reports were made to somebody, somewhere. I'm not aware of them. If these activities were happening at the general command level, definitely they did not necessarily have to trickle down to us, maybe, but I don't know why we were -- we were not informed. And if we were to be informed, it's -- it's not at a personal level. It would have been at UNMO level, maybe from UNMO headquarters all the way down to us, as a team down there, and this did not happen at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on. I've already shown you a number of documents concerning the arming of the units within the enclave, but I'd like to show you a footage now in e-court just to explain to you. According to our information, it was taken on the 10th of July, 1995, in Srebrenica town itself. We've received that piece of information from the OTP, and we have no reason to doubt it. We have no reason to doubt that it was taken on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was -- it is 4D0014.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] We can stop now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, do you recognise the location where this footage was taken?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This should have been, according to what I saw, should have been in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We can see a gas station there. If I remember correctly, since I visited it several times, it is right across the PTT building in Srebrenica; am I correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As I understood from your testimony, you said that on the 9th of July, that is, one day before that, you went to Srebrenica and Potocari together with Major Tetteh. On the 10th of July, you were not in Srebrenica itself as this was taking place. But you also told us that your interpreter, Emir Suljagic, received an order for you -- from you to go to Srebrenica and to report. Since your interpreter was there at the time and informing you on the Srebrenica events, did you receive any information that there was mortar fire being opened on the town from Srebrenica itself on the Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, he did not tell us anything to do with that. But maybe on the 10th, maybe by the time the firing was taking place, I don't know. Maybe that is the time he had already left to come back to -- maybe the timing, if you tell us the timings, I can know whether he had come back to Potocari or not. Also, it's worth noting that by this time, the BiH had already taken some of the weapons from the Bravo Company, so this is a different scenario altogether. It's a different scenario altogether, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, I don't mean to interrupt you, but I only want to know whether, in your sitreps, we can find any information that mortar shells are being fired by the Army of B and H from Srebrenica on the Serb positions and that such fire was being opened from the location of the gas station, or rather, right across the street from the PTT building, if you prefer that.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing like that in our reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I wanted to ask you. We've already seen 4D0002. It is the statement of Ramiz Becirovic, and we agreed that you know him. The date is the 11th of August. I would like to discuss some other parts of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 4D0002 shown in e-court. Let us go to page 4 in the B/C/S and page 5 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As you can see in the second paragraph from the top: [In English] "Agreements on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica, we had to disarm completely. We barely managed to secure some older weapons in disrepair to hand over to UNPROFOR." [Interpretation] Concerning your previous answer, Ramiz Becirovic in his statement says that the weapons handed over to UNPROFOR were old and dysfunctional; and on this footage, we could see a fully functional mortar. Did you know that at the time you were there all of the weapons that had been handed over to UNPROFOR were actually inoperable and old?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were not checking the usability state of the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like us now to go to page 12 in the B/C/S and - excuse me - page 14 in the English, towards the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As you can see, well, in answering Mr. Zivanovic's questions concerning the number of fighters and people who were members of the division, towards the middle of the page, it says: [In English] "A column which sets out that evening was not established, but in my estimate there were between 10.000 and 15.000 people. I had around 6.000 troops, without counting the troops from Zepa." [Interpretation] Do you have any reason to believe that Ramiz Becirovic, who was Chief of Staff of the 28th Division, did not have 6.000 troops, excluding non-fighters and women?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there's -- there's one thing we need maybe to know. Holding 10.000 to 15.000 troops in Srebrenica, as I said yesterday, is a bit difficult. A conventional force of ten to 15 thousand troops definitely is -- it cannot be able to. But what I am saying here is, according to my own interpretation, war is fought from very many fronts, very many fronts, and propaganda is one of them. I'm not saying that this is propaganda, but when you are communicating issues to other authorities, you may want to show how good you are, how organised you are. The opposite is also true, the others on the other side who also try to do the same. What am I trying to say here? Ten thousand to 15 thousand soldiers in an enclave, and especially where we were in Srebrenica itself, we could not have failed to notice that. This, you're saying, is between the 11th and 12th July? 11th and, I think, 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I apologise. You furnished us with the same answer yesterday, stating that you doubt the existence of those. However, potentially, having in mind the number of men within the enclave and the rest, that figure could have been as high as this?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you maybe, if I may request, come up with a date? What date is this? Is it the 11th and 12th, so that I can continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe this is the cause of our misunderstanding. We are talking about a column of men which were trying to break out towards Tuzla. It is Ramiz Becirovic's assessment that the column comprised ten to 15 thousand people, out of which 6.000 were troops, soldiers. That is the piece of information that Ramiz Becirovic is furnishing here, saying that he had 6.000 soldiers at his disposal. This is what is contained in that part of the statement. This is the 11th of July, in the afternoon, when the column started from Susnjari towards Tuzla, trying to break out.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. It is possible, if each and every person -- if each and every person was taken to be a soldier; and maybe even if you're given a weapon, if you're given a gun and you become a soldier, yeah, it is possible to get this number. Especially, when you -- when you're escaping and each and every one is armed, definitely, people in the enclave were more than this. But a conventional -- what I'm disputing is this. A conventional force with 10.000 to 15.000 people, I can't contemplate it being able to be housed in Srebrenica. But if, as I have just said, if you are going to say each and every person, each and every child who is above 15 or so years or so, you give him a gun and he becomes a soldier, each and every old man, I mean, it is possible because the people are there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I won't press any further, but I'd like to go back to a question I had already posed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us please go to page 17 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, one moment. Colonel, we are not actually talking at any time here of a conventional army of between ten to 15 thousand people. I think that was made clear to you by Mr. Lazarevic, and it is clear from the document itself, that ten to 15 thousand people are basically the number of people that made the column or composed the column. When it comes to troops, what Becirovic is saying here that, not counting the troops from Zepa, he had around 6.000 troops. Now, I have heard what you had to say yesterday and what you basically repeated again today. What's not clear in my mind is how you can reconcile the possibility of there being 6.000 individuals who are given a weapon and all of a sudden they become soldiers, so to say, with what you maintained yesterday, saying that the amount of weapons in Srebrenica was minimal or almost nonexistent. If they could arm, give a weapon to 6.000 people, what do you have to say about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, 6.000 people, as far as I can see here, is not necessarily giving each and every person a gun. It could be a weapon, any kind of weapon, any kind of weapon. Like, if there is a pistol, a pistol is not a weapon that one can go fight with. Forming a section is really not necessarily that each and every person has to have a gun. You know, there's no reason -- there's no clear indication that we are getting from this letter that these 6.000 were armed. They can be troops, but not armed. They can be called troops, but not necessarily armed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead, Mr. Lazarevic. I'm not going to ask him any further questions myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: One more thing concerning your statement. I'd like to have your comment about it. At page 17 in the English, in the third paragraph, it reads: [In English] "... Command was located in the area of the old town and the hunters social centre." [Interpretation] Is this not consistent with the document I have shown you recently, where Ramiz Becirovic says that the Division Command was in the Lovac facility, as we can see from this document as well, "Lovac" meaning "hunter" in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't see where you read because it was not shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] It's on page 17, third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's the paragraph starts with, "Throughout these developments," and the next sentence says: "The Division Command was located in the area of the old town and the hunters' social centre ..." It's the second sentence in the third paragraph of.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this consistent with what we saw earlier in another document, where it states that the 28th Division Command was there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's something I did -- I did not know, that the headquarters was located in that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us move on to another topic. On the 10th of July, you were already at the base in Potocari; and according to the information we have, and according to numerous evidence before this Chamber, by that time a great many people -- a great many people started leaving Srebrenica towards Potocari and they began assembling around the base. Is it correct or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, because they are streaming into Potocari and Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The very next day, on the 11th of July, the Serb forces entered the town of Srebrenica, which by that time was empty. People had already left. Does that tally with what you could see at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entry of the Serbs mainly was from the -- the Bratunac side; that is, going via Potocari all the way up towards Srebrenica. This happened that day, so they entered from the Bratunac side. So the ones we are talking about, from entering Srebrenica from anywhere else, we were not aware at that particular moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Perhaps this does not correspond fully to the data I have. But if this is your testimony and your knowledge, I have nothing to observe. However, I'm interested in the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Where were you, exactly, on the 11th of July when the Bosnian Serbs or VRS forces entered Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the 11th, I was in Potocari, Dutch-Bat compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you couldn't see what was happening on the other side of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, that's what I said. I did not see what was happening on the other side, but I saw now the entry from the Bratunac side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think that's clear enough. I mean, he is not contradicting any other evidence there may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Kingori, you said, didn't you, that Serbs went to Srebrenica from the Bratunac side via Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's exactly what I mean. Because I was in Potocari, I could see them going towards Srebrenica from that side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In any case, you arrived in Potocari from Srebrenica. That was the route you took, Srebrenica and Zeleni Jadar, on the 9th?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The direction we took was from Srebrenica down towards Potocari; and Zeleni Jadar, I don't remember. I mean, we were not going towards that direction. Zeleni Jadar, I think, is in exactly the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. It was a mistake in the transcript or I may have misspoken, in which case I apologise. I'm asking these questions for the following reason: Do you know who it was that decided, for the people from Srebrenica who were there on the 10th, to take the same route you did for Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, there's nobody who told them, but it's common sense that the safer place was now towards where the UNPROFOR is. It's common sense, so I think that is -- that is exactly what they followed. Even ourselves, that is the route we followed. We found that we would be safer when we are, all of us, together in one particular place, and especially when we are in a battalion headquarter where there is a bit of defence and where the BSA would think twice before -- before hitting, because at least they know we are there. There's nothing we are going to do to them, and that is a safer place. That is why these -- the Muslims also maybe thought that is wiser, to go towards that direction, where they think they have safety and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So if I understand your answer correctly, since it was quite a lengthy one, you say that no one actually took the decision to go from Srebrenica to the Potocari base. It was just a reasonable line of thinking that made those people go there; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's asked and answered, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Let us, please, go back to Ramiz Becirovic's statement, 4D02, page 12. We've spoken about this already a lot already. Page 12 in the English. [In English] Can we scroll it down a bit just to make sure the witness can see the lower part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, towards the bottom of this page, there's the word "UNPROFOR." This is five or six lines from the bottom: [In English] "That UNPROFOR soldiers were directing the inhabitants to Potocari. When I asked why, I was told that they, too, had the intention of moving on to Potocari." [Interpretation] Did you know anything to indicate that UNPROFOR soldiers were sending people from Srebrenica to Potocari or telling them to go there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not have such information at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is very similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But can we please just move on to page 14 of the English, the top of the page. It's the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Again, I will ask you this: Did you know about this? You see, the second sentence from the top of the page: [In English] "I ordered the signalmen to go out on the hill and establish communication with the Corps Command. We remained behind and determined the manner of movement, the sequence of units, security methods, and reconnoitering. At the rear, the column would head towards Tuzla. "The order was issued that the entire civilian population located there set off, but they were free to decide whether they would go with us or head towards UNPROFOR." [Interpretation] Did you have information to the effect that the population from Srebrenica had been ordered to go to Potocari by the Corps Command? Did you know about that? A simple "yes" or "no" will do, please. There's no need to go any further into this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: But, Mr. President, I just don't think that's what's represented in the plain language of the document, as I read it. It appears that they were given a choice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, I can -- I can understand. They had a choice whether to go to Potocari or to go through the woods, but not to make any other decisions, because here it says the order was issued that the entire civilian population located there set off, and that was my question. They are free to decide whether they would go "with us," meaning with the army through the woods, or head towards UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead and answer the question, please, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's clearly indicated here that they were not forced to go to any direction. They were free to either follow these guys to the -- towards Tuzla or go to -- to Potocari. They were free to make their own choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This document shows clearly that there was no third option for them; namely, to stay where they were. That was not an option, was it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not indicated here, but that does not mean that it was not there. Only that, as I said earlier, if I may have to repeat it, their direction towards -- they had to move to a safe place. The issue here is safety and security, safety and security. And if it were me, definitely I would have moved towards Potocari because I could believe that it was more secure and safer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us just clarify one thing. In essence, you've answered the question already, but let's just dispel any doubts that may remain. Did you, and I mean the UNMOs, the Dutch-Bat Command representatives of military or civilian authorities, have any sort of meeting about what would become of the civilians should they go, should they stay, if they were going, where would they be going to? Did you discuss anything like that during your meeting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could just have a time frame for this, because these decisions were potentially taken at different locations at different times for different reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] By all means, by all means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The time period that I have in mind would be, roughly speaking, somewhere around the 8th and 9th, the 10th, possibly the 11th of July, over those four days. Because we know that on the 11th of July, or by the 11th of July, the population of Srebrenica had moved to Potocari already. Were there any debate in those days as to what the civilians would be doing? Would they be going, would they be staying, and I mean of course in terms of your own personal experience, attending any such meetings, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what there is is that we had no meeting to discuss or even direct the people to go to any place. That was not discussed anywhere that they would go directly towards a certain direction. In fact, what really happened is that when the people started streaming towards Srebrenica, we realised that it's becoming an issue, that many people are going towards there. But there was no meeting that I can recall that we discussed where these people were to go. The only thing we did is when they came in and they filled the whole Dutch-Bat compound, that is, that whole factory, we decided that, for the rest, we would place them next to the road just short of the Potocari Dutch-Bat compound. But on where they were to be taken, I mean, the direction they were to take from Srebrenica, we never had such a meeting that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. I would like to see another short video clip. You may be able to identify a number of faces from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is P02047 from Srebrenica. The footage was taken on the 10th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you that particular portion of the footage, and we'll stop at a certain point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the 10th of July, 1995 footage from Potocari. You saw the subtitles and you could follow what was being said in the footage. My apologies. This is Srebrenica, not Potocari. I seem to have misspoken again. The footage was taken at Srebrenica on the 10th of July. You saw a man there saying, and the subtitles reflected that, "They are forcing us to go to Potocari. Block the road." He is now addressing the civilians. Can you tell us who this man could have had in mind when he said, "They are forcing us to go to Potocari"? Why was he addressing the people there, asking them to block the road? What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, without some further foundation, I think this question really just calls for a sheer speculation as to why somebody might be doing something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's move to your next question, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Let me just finish this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, on the 10th of July, in the town of Srebrenica itself, there are no Serb soldiers, not yet. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no Serb soldiers at that time in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and it seems to follow from that that the Serb Army could not possibly have been the one to order anyone to leave Srebrenica, which is what seems to follow from your answer. Would that seem to be a fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it would be towards something there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can safely go to your next question. Mr. Lazarevic, when you realise that a witness knows next to nothing on a particular event or on a particular chapter in the events that we're talking about, and you have and we have other evidence that we have heard, why waste your time on him? So at the end of the day, what is he going to tell you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll move on to something else. Can we please have P0009.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You see, Colonel, this is a letter written by the president of the Presidency, Osman Suljic, and we know that you know who he was. He was the president of the Presidency of Srebrenica Municipality. He sent this letter on the 7th of July, 1995, to President Ramiz Becirovic and the General of the Army, General Rasim Delic. We can see the date on the face of this document. If you look at the lower half of the document, you will be going through the entire document, but the portion that I'm interested in is the paragraph where it reads: "The civilian authorities were left with the last unpopular step of saving the population. It is stressed that a meeting at the level of state and military organs of the RBH should organised with the aggressor side with the aim at fighting and possibility to open a corridor to be used by the population to move to the nearest free territory of the RBH under the control of the international players." This document was produced by Osman Suljic. It's a letter that he wrote. Can we use this to infer that as early as the 9th of July, 1995, the possibility was reviewed of moving the entire civilian population out of the Srebrenica enclave, and that, in fact, this is something that was done by the local authorities?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this happened, or this letter is written, though the time is not indicated, on the 9th of July. This is the date we left Srebrenica. That's the time we left the PTT building for Potocari . And as it is indicated in my statement, at this time these people felt very insecure, after we gave our intention to depart from Srebrenica to Potocari. That insecurity may have caused a lot of panic, which is true, and definitely they did not know where else to go, who else to talk to, and maybe even the ultimate place where they would be headed for. This letter, as you can see, I think it was one out of desperation, where the president did not know what else to do with the population. But he's saying that they may find a possibility to open a corridor for the population to move to the nearest free territory; that is, to ensure that the people are safe. In essence, the -- the way we should be looking at this issue is that the enclave had already been encroached by the Bosnian Serb Army, and this was from all sides, almost all sides. It's like the Muslims were being crushed in one place, sort of, and they had now to look for a possible exist from the problems that they were already in, the bombardment, the harassment, and the possible decimation by the BSA, because these guys were really pounding on Srebrenica in a way that they really do not want anyone to -- I mean, they wanted the whole enclave, all the people inside there, either to be -- to be killed or to vacate, one of them, and it is indicated even in my statement. So what I'm trying to say here is that they had to look a safe way out, they had to look for a safe way out, not necessarily because of their own will to leave the enclave, but because they are forced by circumstances under which the bombardment was happening. They were being bombarded, and they were left with no option but to try to escape from this place. Otherwise, they would be killed all of them together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I would like to ask you something, though. My question was a very simple one. Basically, it would have elicited a yes-or-no answer. It is not my intention to offend you or to interrupt any of the answers you think to provide, although it is, as it happens, filled with speculation and mere assumptions. But can we please just try to wrap this up as quickly and expeditiously as possible. Otherwise, I will not be able to comply with my remit here, and I will be leaving no time for my learned friends from the other Defence teams. Please bear this in mind for the benefit of the Chamber and all the other Defence teams, if you can. Now I'll continue to follow the timeline of your statement to the OTP. This is page 8 of the B/C/S version and the English version as well. You testified that on the 11th of July, 1995, a meeting was held which you personally did not attend. The meeting was held between General Mladic and Colonel Karremans, but you clearly state that you don't remember who called that meeting, who asked for that meeting. Was it the VRS or Colonel Karremans, you're not sure. You remember that portion of your statement to the OTP, do you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like us again to look at some footage which might be able to jog your memory a little. You'll watch it in e-court now, and you will hear what those two participants had to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you heard General Mladic ask Karremans what he wanted. He says, "You called the meeting, you asked for the meeting." Would this jog your memory? Would this help you remember who was the first to ask for a meeting, and I'm referring to the meeting that was eventually held on the 11th at the Fontana Hotel in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish you would play it again. I can't give the voice to whichever person, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you this, sir. We do have a transcript of this exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is P02048, and it's page 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to interrupt you, but again, where do you think are you going to get? Where do you think you're getting? You have the tape and you have Mladic speaking and saying. Is his testimony going to change anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] I was only trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But at the end of the day, even if he told you, "No, it was Mladic who was at the meeting," is it going to change anything? What Mladic says on the tape is what he says, I mean, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour, maybe I don't -- I really don't need to insist on this, of course. However, I notice that the witness couldn't remember certain details, and this was just for the purpose to refresh his memory. However, I can skip to something else. But then I will first ask the witness -- of course, he wasn't present there, but I will ask him only one question in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, sir, were I to tell you that the issue of moving the refugees who were at Potocari to Tuzla territory was first raised by Colonel Karremans, were I to tell you that he was the first to bring this up with Mladic and ask him to talk on behalf of the civilians in Potocari about moving them to Tuzla, would that be consistent with what you actually witnessed there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you go back to my statement, you will see that I indicated that there is a time that I talked to General Ratko Mladic, and the plan was if the civilians, because now the UN had to move and General Mladic had already indicated that the UN must leave that place, where were the civilians to go to, then we said that, and I remember I'm the one who told General Mladic, that the UN would prepare to evacuate, to remove the people from there because they cannot be left there. They would not be safe. They will not be -- is it working? Yeah. They will not be safe in that place. So when I asked him, when I told him that it is the intention of the UN to remove the people from there, to provide buses, the general said that he's already been able to get his own buses. He will get his own buses and bring them over, to pick the people from Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, it is not my intention to interrupt you, but I do have the questions here about that. I just wanted to follow the timeline and then sort of link these up. I promise that I'll be asking you further questions about the meeting and what you said to Mladic at the time. My intention was to ask you whether you, in fact, knew that Colonel Karremans was the first to raise this, but you weren't there, yourself; therefore, I'm not pressing the matter. I'd like us to look at something else now. This is a document that you produced. It's an UNMO report dated the 11th of July, 1995, Attachment 16 to your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is P00510.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you have that in front of you, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's dated the 11th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Indeed. To the extent that I can see, it was dispatched at 1745 hours; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: At paragraph 2, in the last line of this report, it says: [In English] "... Tuzla is a possibility in the coming days." [Interpretation] At that right, sir, that's what it says, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where did you read that, para 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] It's second paragraph, last sentence: "... Movement out of the enclave."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're saying the refugees are moving to the northern part of the enclave and the food situation is becoming critical? I don't know where that is on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and next sentence?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The movement out of enclave towards Tuzla region is a possibility in the coming days."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one I'm referring to. [Interpretation] Can you confirm that that's what the sitrep says, the one that left at 1745; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is an UNMO assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Believe me, there's nothing tricky about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Should we take a break? I mean, it's 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau, having followed cross-examination of Mr. Lazarevic of over two hours already, how much time do you think you will need?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, one hour and a half, I think. I'm ready to make an effort if we must finish with the witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We must. I said that loud and clear yesterday. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I really would like my hour and a half as well, Your Honour. The -- could I make this remark? I'd rather have done it in the absence of the witness. But since I addressed the Court very briefly yesterday, I've had an opportunity to look at a document that he brought to The Hague, which was disclosed on Tuesday, and I would like to ask him about it at some length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Lazarevic, how long --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more time do you think you require, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, during this break, I really looked at the questions that I prepared, and I deleted a large number of questions from my list. However, we are progressing relatively slowly, I have to admit this, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's certainly not the Trial Chamber's fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to need -- yes, of course, and I really was doing my best to organise my questions in order to speed up things, but it's very difficult with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. You have to conclude in ten minutes, Mr. Lazarevic. You've been already two hours and a half, so you have ten minutes, and the rest of the time needs to be divided between you, Mr. Josse and Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I please confer for one minute with Madame Fauveau and Mr. Josse, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, right now I have very limited re-examination, but considering that we've got what I anticipate to be two substantial cross-examinations, I may need a few more minutes, based on some of the questions that are asked. I just can't predict that, but I will need some perhaps 15 minutes, I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We had originally put an hour down and we reserved 30 minutes, so we certainly are not waiving that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Trial Chamber are saying the witness has to be finished today, then clearly that's a decision and we'll all have to abide by it. But if the witness is going to go over to Monday, then, in my submission, there is no point doing this with unseemly haste, particularly bearing in mind how this trial has proceeded hitherto. I say that with the greatest of respect. But if it's going to end today, then clearly there won't be time for any re-examination and we will -- we will all tailor our cross-examinations accordingly, if that's the order of the Court. But if not, then, as I say, there is no point, to use the same expression, doing this with unseemly haste, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we will do is the following: You'll have 20 more minutes, Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Josse and Ms. Fauveau, you will have one hour each. You will have 15 minutes for re-examination, which means we won't be able to finish by quarter to 2:00, which ultimately means that we will reconvene in this same courtroom at a quarter past 2.00 and continue from there. All right? Yes, 20 minutes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, if you could please issue an instruction to the witness just to answer with short answers, if possible, of course, because otherwise I don't know how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually, I will do two things. I will do that. Witness, please try to be concise as much as you can in your answers, and you, Mr. Lazarevic, please avoid long-winded questions or going around in circles when you can put a very straightforward question, because that is what has been happening today and yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will obey to this ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Colonel, we saw the sitrep already and when it was sent. Can you confirm to me that the issue of evacuation of the refugees was discussed and arranged before Colonel Karremans met with General Mladic at 8.00 in the evening that day? Please answer with a "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no indication that that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In the report, it says: [In English] "Movement out of the enclave is a possibility in the coming days." [Interpretation] That is what I had in mind concerning to that part of sitrep. Does that change your answer in any way?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it does not, because this is an assessment by the SMO. An assessment is not necessarily coming out of a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to the arrival of Serb forces in Potocari. You've testified before this Chamber that according to what you could see, the first soldiers to enter Potocari wore black uniforms. They were followed by others, by other soldiers in different uniforms. Testifying in the Krstic trial, you said that a group of soldiers entered the base to check whether there were any BiH soldiers inside. You also said that you knew some of those people and that one of them was Major Nikolic; your interpreter, Petar; and Colonel Vukovic, and that the whole thing lasted for about a quarter of an hour. Do you stand by your answer?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the Prosecutor and your testimony so far, I understood that you knew Major Nikolic from earlier. It is the person we know by the name of "Momir Nikolic," just to confirm; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person I know is the one we were calling "Major Nikolic." I don't know the other names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your statement, this Major Nikolic, at page 3 in the B/C/S and the same page in the English, you described him as follows: "Major Nikolic was the commander of the local unit of the BSA. He at least presented himself as the commander." [Interpretation] Can you confirm that here today as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He told us that is the local commander of the BSA in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You saw Major Nikolic in Potocari on the 12th and the 13th of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to the 13th of July. According to your statement to the Prosecutor at page 10, you say that the evacuation of the population from Potocari began on the 13th of July, around 7.00 a.m. Can you confirm that here today?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I can't see a copy of the statement, but I think that is the date started.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. My learned friend, Mr. Prosecutor, can verify that, whether I quoted it precisely. Another thing concerning this issue: On the 13th of July, 1995, did the evacuation process begin prior to the arrival of the Serb forces in Potocari? Did the members of the Dutch-Bat initiate evacuation alone, without the presence of any Serb forces, on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If I told you that there is testimony here of a Dutch soldier who participated in it and who said that they, themselves, initiated the evacuation, would that change your answer?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will not, because I saw it. I saw the evacuation, I was there as a military observer, and I know what I saw and witnessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to clarify the previous statement with respect to the evacuation starting at 0700 on the 13th, I have read the reference in the witness statement and I would just ask my friend to make a clarification and actually read the portion of the statement, because it is slightly different and it may make a difference. I don't want there to be any confusion on the record, and I can just state it. It says: "The next day, 13 July, the evacuation resumed at 0700," and I think the question was "The evacuation started." I just didn't want there to be any lack of clarity about when it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] I'm fine with what my colleague said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, so let's move on to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I said it in B/C/S. This is why it occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that on the 13th, at a certain point in time, you left Potocari for Srebrenica and then returned, whereupon you met Major Nikolic at the base on the 13th. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, if I understood the gist of your testimony, those who were evacuated first were those who were outside the base in Potocari; and after that phase of evacuation was completed, only then the people who were within the base at Potocari were evacuated. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Testifying before this Tribunal on the 14th of December, you, talking about the sitrep of the 12th of July, said that there were some 10.000 refugees within the base and some 20.000 without the base, explaining that in the building of the base itself, there were some 5.000 people, and an additional 5.000 within the general compound, a wider area of the base. Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not remember it getting as such, because generally those who were inside the -- the compound were five -- you know, around 5.000 or so; and those outside, the ones who were 20. But the figure inside could have been between 5.000 and 7.000, somewhere there. I'm not trying to contradict. I'm just saying the possibility of it being that figure. But there was no inside, the workshop, that is, the main building and outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In order for the Chamber to have a clearer picture of the situation, I wanted to show a short footage so that we could see the actual area. It is a footage made by one of the members of the Dutch-Bat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, you can stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you make out the facilities we saw in this short footage?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, I wanted to say that we saw the footage from 000104 to 00010 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 001010.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... some six seconds in the footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You can see from here the Dutch base; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: To the right of the entrance, there is a Dutch observation post; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In the left-hand corner of the screen, we can see the building which you termed "the white house" in your testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Were you present when the evacuation began, the evacuation of those who were within the compound of Dutch-Bat; that is to say, at the outset?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't get the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat. When people began being evacuated from the base, were you present there at the very beginning of the evacuation from the base or had you gone to Srebrenica by that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the time the evacuation started from inside the base I was, I was around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. That is what I wanted to hear. When the evacuation began from the base, you saw Major Nikolic there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, Major Nikolic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He had a list in his hands with certain names. He said that those people, in his belief, were war criminals, according to the information the Bratunac Brigade had at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, he had a list. He had a list that he was checking through.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Having in mind the still before us, we can see that the white house is close to the entrance, and the men leaving the base had to cross the road and make their way to the white house. I apologise, I apologise. It should have read "across the road from the entrance of the base."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't get what you mean, because for the people to get inside that white house, the people who were going there are the ones who are being collected from outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The people, the men who were inside the base were leaving through the gate, by the way of the entrance we can see here. What I wanted to ask you is this: When they crossed the road, they immediately come up to the white house. They are being sent there, those which had been taken?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have not stated anywhere that those from inside the base were taken to the white house. There is nowhere that I've stated that, because I did not see them being taken to the white house from inside the compound. The ones I talked about were the ones who were being picked from outside the compound to the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on to my next question. Were you familiar with the fact that inside the base, a list was made of men who were inside the base? Major Franken provided a sheet of paper on which the list of men who were inside the base were included. Did you know of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know -- what I knew about was that Major Nikolic was coming through with a list and checking from amongst the men who were there, who corresponded with the name and whatever he had in his list. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you don't know of the Franken list, the list comprising the Muslims who were inside the base itself? You don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, the document -- or rather, the footage that we saw is 4D131.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Answering Mr. Zivanovic's questions, you mentioned Hasan Nuhanovic, who was your interpreter. At page 11 of your statement to the Prosecution, in both the English and the B/C/S version, you said that Hasan Nuhanovic asked you to sign a document in which it was stated that his family left the base on the 13th of July, having been ordered to do so by the Dutch officers. However, you don't know whether they indeed left and under what circumstances. Do you still stand by what you said, that you were not present when Mr. Nuhanovic's family left the base in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I still stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show another footage, please. It is 4D00132. For the record, it begins with 004226 to 004330.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Is this Hasan Nuhanovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You could see the English subtitles, and Hasan Nuhanovic says that three Dutch-Bat soldiers, together with three UNMOs that he used to be interpreter to, arrived, and he was told that his family had to leave the base area in Potocari. Is what Hasan Nuhanovic said correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just to be completely clear about this, three UNMOs. I'm not saying it's true, what Hasan Nuhanovic said, but let us try and identify those three people. It is you, Major Dehan, and Major Tetteh. Those were the only three UNMOs who were in Srebrenica at the time; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I mean is that, myself, I never witnessed that. I was not there on whatever he is talking about. So as far as I'm concerned, it did not happen. I did not see it. I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. According to your statement at page 11 of both the English and the B/C/S, you said that the entire evacuation was completed on the 13th, in the afternoon; and that, after that, a delegation comprising senior officers inspected the complex, among whom you recognised Major Nikolic and Colonel Acamovic. Colonel Acamovic introduced himself as a special envoy or representative of General Mladic, in charge of the evacuation. Do you stand by that answer?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Another thing: You were there when the evacuation was completed. Was there a large pile, a heap of clothes, discarded clothes, that belonged to the people who had been evacuated from the base?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were clothes, and the ones I talked about in my statement are the ones left outside the white house, after those detained in the white house left. That is one that I talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. However, I'm asking you about the base area. Was there a heap of clothes there as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, inside the base area, I never noticed a heap of clothes or anything, only that there were -- it was littered with a lot of dark papers everywhere. It was littered with a lot of things. But a heap of clothes like witnessed, you know, outside the white house, I did not see it myself.
