utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Referring to Major Nikolic in the Krstic case, on the 13th of July, it is page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please repeat the page reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] I apologise to the interpreters. [Interpretation] I am referring to 1874 and 1875, the pages of the transcript in the Krstic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It has to do with the events of the 13th of July, and I will read it in English, that is, your answer concerning Major Nikolic: [In English] "He was there almost throughout." [Interpretation] Let me say that you saw him in and outside the Dutch-Bat base; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honours, I believe that I need, literally, five to ten more minutes. There is nothing more. This has speeded up, and, really, I think that all these questions that I have are highly relevant to the indictment and deal with particular charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will have seven minutes, seven minutes, not a second more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour is very generous.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, Colonel, I would like to ask you specifically about OPs. I came across certain references in sitreps to you reporting on Dutch-Bat OPs. I want to know about Observation Post Papa. That's what your reports reflect, even up to which point in time Papa OP was being used. Up until which point in time did the Dutch-Bat people remain there, and when did they withdraw from their OP to the one near the yellow bridge?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that was the last OP to be -- for the Dutch-Bat to evacuate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Of course, you can't pinpoint the date for us, can you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot. I cannot remember the actual dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. On the 13th and 14th of December, you gave evidence before this Chamber. This is 19254 and 19921. You were shown footage of a person who you said spoke little English and was helping you by doing some interpretation for you. You say that it can be seen in the footage that he was wearing a UN bulletproof vest. You remember that; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: About that same person, you testified in the Krstic trial; and on 1860 of the transcript, you categorically stated this, and I'll quote in English: [In English] "I am sure it had been stolen from some of the Dutch soldiers." [Interpretation] Do you still maintain the same thing today?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "May," the word is "may." "May have been stolen from the Dutch-Bat soldiers." It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. That is good enough for my purposes, because I don't have much time left, but there's something I'd like to show you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is OTP Exhibit number P01936, page 62. That is the e-court reference.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the counsel repeat the exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: By all means. It's P01936, page 62.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You see this shot. Is this the same person you talked about? That's all I'm trying to find out. It's the young man on the right with the blue UN bulletproof vest.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. This is the man I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Were I to tell you that Dutch soldiers never had any light blue bulletproof vests but rather camouflage ones, how would that affect your conclusion that this bulletproof vest may have been stolen from the UN? Would that change your conclusion, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The point is that from the UN, I think my main concern was not whether it's Dutch-Bat but the UN. This is an UN vest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You're entirely certain of what you are saying; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that means a changing, but what this means is these are UN -- UN vests. The BSA also never used anything blue. It is not in their inventory, but the UN had the blue bulletproof vests.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well, very well. There's just one more thing that I'd like us to look at. In your testimony on the 14th of December before this Tribunal, page 19290, you were watching a video clip and you noticed a person in the footage: [In English] "This is not a UN soldier, but he has a blue helmet." [Interpretation] Do you remember that or would you perhaps like to be shown the relevant portion again?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please do, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. This is P2 -- P02074, and the time reference is 01.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You'll be seeing that on your screen in a moment, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] We can stop now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We spoke about this point in time, and you talked about this person, and you said that he was wearing a blue helmet but that this was no UN soldier. Do you now remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you stand by that statement that you made; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Were I to tell you that the person wearing the blue helmet was Vincentus Egbert and that he identified himself as a member of Dutch-Bat in this footage, would that perhaps do anything to change your opinion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I don't object to the question itself, other than that's not the testimony. It was another individual who identified himself, Eelco Koster, not Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] I apologise, my mistake. My colleague is right. My colleague is 100 per cent right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. It's being put to you that actually that individual came here and identified himself as being a member of Dutch-Bat. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, now, the -- the point is that I don't remember whether it is this person. I don't know whether we can see the whole clip or whether there's the possibility of seeing someone else in a blue -- a blue helmet who is not a Dutch soldier, because I believe there was and I saw one like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: By all means, sir, but please accept what I'm telling you. I've seen the footage many times. We could, of course, do that. With the exception of this gentleman and yourself, nobody else appears to be wearing a blue helmet in this footage. However, I'll withdraw my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's better. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions left. During your evidence before this Tribunal, you spoke a great deal about the white house. Let me clarify a point in relation to that. You said you went to this white house. You talked about what happened there, something to do with General Mladic outside the white house. You talked about the distribution of beer, fruit juice, sweets, and such, at the white house. While you were there, did you actually count the people who were brought to the white house?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question you're asking, I really was not there counting the people who were going in; and at that particular moment, we were seeing those who were inside the house, not those who were coming in. So the issue of counting, I think, may not arise at this moment, because I was not counting those who were going in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When you say "we," are you talking about yourself, you as an individual, or are you talking about other UNMOs as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, I mean I'm talking about UNMOs. And if I can be specific, then I can talk about myself, in that when we went there with the general -- when I went there with General Ratko Mladic, myself, I never counted the people who were going in. And at that particular moment, as I've just said, there was no issue of people going in, because when we went there to see them, they were already inside the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just another question. That is practically my second-to-last question. Did you perhaps count the people who were taken from the white house to the buses?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I did not count.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You see, there has been evidence before this Tribunal, more specifically one of the Dutch-Bat officers testified, Major Franken to be specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the benefit of my learned friends, I will provide a transcript reference, 4297 and 4298.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Major Franken spoke about this, and he said that he was the one who put an UNMO in charge of counting the people who were brought to the white house, as well as those who were leaving the white house to be taken to the buses. Then on 2675, he goes on to say this: "The numbers of those counted tallied. In other words, the same number of people was brought to the white house as those that were taken out." Is that your experience, namely, that one of the UNMOs was monitoring the process whereby people were being brought to the white house and taken out of the white house? This seems to be the information that was forwarded to Dutch-Bat.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, for one, Major Franken could not order the military observers to do anything. That is a fact. We were the same rank. He could not order us to do anything. Secondly, we were of different commands. We were military observers. He was from Dutch-Bat. So the issue of ordering any observer, that's not right. Secondly, the -- the counting of the men that were going into the white house, as far as I'm concerned, I don't think he did that. I mean, we did that, as observers. And even when they were going out, I don't remember -- okay. If I talk about myself, I don't remember, myself, counting those people. But I was there when they were going to the buses. I was personally there, but we were not counting the people. I do not remember, myself, giving out a figure of this number of men who left -- I mean, who, as we were counting them, were going into the buses. I don't remember doing that. It's only that, if I may add -- if I'm allowed to add, it's only that we were counting the busloads when they were leaving. We were counting the busloads, and we could estimate the number of people going out, because for the busloads, we knew capacity of the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But this is your personal experience. Are you certain about your colleagues? Did one of them perhaps do just that, unbeknownst to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe anyone, any other observer counted the people, one, two, three, whatever, as they boarded the buses or even as they were going into the white house. That, I don't believe. But we counted the busloads.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Colonel. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: My name is Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic, and I represent General Ivetic? Is it right that before getting on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, you were working in the Kenya Air Force?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: As an officer, as an Air Force officer, did you not have an experience in calculating trajectory and craters?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a trained military officer, that was part of our training, and we were ongoing in that training and we knew how to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, but you told us that you joined the Kenyan Air Force in 1977. From that moment on, therefore, you were no longer working with these matters on those things?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After joining in 1977, as a soldier, I trained and became a fully-trained soldier. In 1985, I went back for cadets officers' course, a one-year cadets officers' course, which enriched me with all these capabilities. That included even battle camps and everything else that has something to do with war. All the major support weapons, everything, you name it, I learned about them. In 1987, I went to the United States of America, where I trained on all major weapons, including even the ones which were not being used in Srebrenica or in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including even the aircrafts themselves, the kind of weapons they carried, and even the artillery, as part of the supply chain. And immediately after that, in 1988, I did the Grade 3 staff course. This is staff and command course. That included everything to do with weaponry, the fighting in battle areas, and also the -- all the weapon systems that I needed in any weapon theatre, including the ones we have in the military and the ones we do not have, because they are also needed. Then in 1988, I went to India, where I trained on similar issues, but now at a slightly advanced level. So when I say that I am familiar with these kind of weapons, I may not be 100 per cent, and also my employment may not be in the infantry or any specific arm, but that does not mean I do not have a general knowledge of this kind of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Very well. But you do confirm to us that for approximately 20 years, or 18 to be more precise, you worked as an Air Force officer?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I've just explained that in plain terms; and though the normal employment will be on the specific job that you do, that does not mean that you do not know the other issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, I guess you answered my question. When you would go out to analyse craters, what was the role of the interpreters during this analysis?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not carrying interpreters to help us in analysing. We were carrying interpreters to do their role as interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you were analysing craters, did you take pictures of the craters?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think -- I think we were doing -- we had cameras, I think. I can't remember very well, but I think we had cameras that we used to take the photos. Yeah, I think we had. We were taking them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you be able to tell me where these pictures are right now or what happened to those pictures when you left the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, some of the photos we would attach to the sitreps when we were sending them over, or sent them as an attachment; and where they are, where the copies are, I really cannot tell now.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you were analysing craters, would you include in your daily report the analysis, the results of the analysis, or were you sending a specific report on the crater analysis that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At times, Your Honour, we would include both the results and also the measurements that we took, but what was required most was the -- the analysis itself, what did we find.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to show you now very quickly 5D502. Before this document is posted on the screen, this is a demilitarisation agreement that my colleague showed you yesterday. What I would like to know is the following: Before arriving to Srebrenica or when you were in Srebrenica, were you made aware of this agreement? Did you ever see it while you were there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was aware of the demilitarised areas in the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Concerning the document itself, I don't remember seeing it or reading it, myself, but that does not mean that it was not there. I'm not sure whether it was there or not, but I don't remember, you know, going through it myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At any rate, this agreement was not something that was extremely important to you. You do not have a memory of knowing or finding out what these clauses were at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a frequency interference or something. The interpreters have some problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I am hearing that, too. I don't know what's the cause of it, where it's emanating from, but there is definitely an interference. I can't hear it now, I mean, so let's proceed; and then if it becomes a problem, we'll try and sort it out. Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, should I repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the question is there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't see it. I don't have it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Line 17 on page 57: "At any rate, this agreement was not something that was extremely important to you. You do not have a memory of knowing or finding out what these clauses were at the time?" This is what is being put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the fact that I do not see these, I did not read, I did not personally read these -- this agreement, does not mean that it was not important. But at least most of the information contained herein, I was aware, and we had been briefed on the issues that, you know, are being referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: A lot of talk was held on the disarmament of Srebrenica, which didn't mean that you didn't know that weapons were coming into Srebrenica. But what I would like to know is whether you knew that the Serbs suspected that weapons were carried to Srebrenica, because Serbs were complaining about the arrival of weapons to Srebrenica, did they not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question is a bit -- I don't -- I don't really get it, but the weapons that you are talking about --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, the question is rather complicated. I will try to simplify it. You are right. Is it right to say that Serbs complained about the arrival and the transportation of weapons into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Your Honour, we're really having problems with this interference. Could you please call a technician, maybe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. You could call a technician, please. I am not hearing it now, but of course it doesn't mean that you don't have the interference over there. We are calling a technician. Okay. Thank you. Can you answer the question, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I really do not remember much concerning -- concerning the complaints by the BSA on weapons going into -- into Srebrenica. I think maybe - I'm not very sure - but maybe once, but sincerely I cannot remember very well -- very well of the complaints of weapons going into there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This complaint regarded the arrival of weapons via helicopters; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was ones complaining about a helicopter going into the enclave. That was raised by the BSA. That I can remember, and they talked about them bringing it down. And after that, I remember, and it's in my statement somewhere, that although the BiH denied that, I saw Ramiz, you know, limping, and maybe that is -- that was the cause of the -- his -- his problems on the left -- I think left or right leg, I can't remember which one. But, yeah, there was a complaint about a helicopter going in there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But the fact that you saw Ramiz Becirovic injured contributed to veracity of the Serbian complaint. It corroborated that complaint, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you try to get more information from the municipality authorities or military authorities after seeing that Ramiz Becirovic was injured?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. As observers, we asked them actually the cause of his limping. In fact, we asked them if actually the helicopter was brought down, and they denied. They said there was nothing like that. But after we saw that Ramiz was limping, we asked them what was the cause, and they said. Even though at time that he was hospitalised, we were told; and when he came out, that is the time we discovered he was limping. When asked them, they said it's a normal injury, and that's what they told us. We could not be able to go further into it because we didn't know now who else to ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 5D214, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is an official report from the 28th Division, the Security Department. It's a report written on the 22nd of May, 1995, and you can see, at -- towards the middle of the page, that this is an official report drafted on the 17th of May, 1995, with regard to a helicopter that was hit during the night of 6th to 7th May, 1995. If I understand correctly, you never saw these reports before. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true, I didn't. I never saw this report at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If you look at the top part of the page, you can see that it says "28th Division Command, Security Department." Do you know where this Security Department of the 28th Division was situated physically?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, these names, I don't know where it was -- where it was located. I don't know the actual location. All I know is that 28th Division, which was later changed to 8-OG, they had a command net at our building; that is, PTT.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this interference is really bothering the interpreters. I'm terribly sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What happened with the technicians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They are already in there. Yes. I can understand the interpreters getting annoyed with this, because it's annoying me as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are suggesting to take the break now, 25 minutes now, so that in the meantime they try and fix this nuisance. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: After seeing Ramiz Becirovic injured, did you tell you superiors that a possibility existed that weapons had been brought to the enclave? Did you make a report on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think the problem is the witness can't hear anything at all. I had to reset my set presumably because of the problem we had before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Same case here, but it was easy to realise. Can you repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, after you saw that Ramiz Becirovic was wounded, did you send a report to your superiors regarding a possibility that weapons be brought into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we sent a report concerning the possibility that that helicopter that crashed could have carried Becirovic, but I don't remember indicating anything to do with -- with the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You declared that your offices were in the post office building. You talked about the centre of communications, and earlier you told us that the Security Department was also in the same building. Did you tell your superiors that you were in the same building as the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was known, it was known. We had found the building there, the observers there, housed there, and the communication was still there. So it was all known from the beginning that the communication was there in the same building with the observers.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, I understand what you're telling us, but I would like to know if you or one of your colleagues, while you were there, did you ever inform your superiors about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, there is a report somewhere concerning that. The same building that we were in is the one that was holding the communication equipments of the BSA -- of the BiH. There is a report on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Neither you, neither your superiors, thought that you should be in a building without any military presence of one of the parties which took part in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the hiring of buildings where observers are housed, that is where the officers are. As far as I'm concerned, I was not involved in it; so me, I just went where the observers were staying.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You also told us that you did not know if there were any brigades in the enclave, the brigade that belonged to the 28th Division. If you did not know that the brigades were there, you could not know where your headquarters were, could you -- where their headquarters were situated?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really, I don't think you want me to go back into saying the way the organisation was or where the -- because I already talked about the 28th Division and the 8-OG. So I know about them, and I really don't know what you want me to say concerning this.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Since you don't know where the militaries or the soldiers in the enclave were situated, how can you know that the eventual Serb targets were civilian and not military?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is something that I've already said before, and that is, the targeting of the enclave, whether there was any military objective or not, the way the shelling was done was definitely aimed at the residents of that place. The residents, as far as I was concerned, were mainly civilians. Most of them were civilians, even if there was some armed brigades. Definitely, the major was civilians in that enclave, and so my -- my conscience is very clear that the target was there, not necessarily just the communication building. The whole enclave was being shelled, and the whole enclave did not have communications centres. It did not have the military people distributed in each and every corner of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know if Dutch-Bat members thought that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were shooting on their own people, that they suspected this on at least one occasion?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, unless you tell me the occasion, because, you know, Dutch-Bat were doing their own things other than where--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But, Colonel, this is something which you either heard about or you didn't. If you didn't, there's no point in telling you when or which occasion it was. Did you ever hear of such a case while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only time that there was suspected to be -- you know, we suspected that maybe something like that happened was when there was an infiltration by the BSA into the enclave. We said maybe also on the other side, the BiH could have done it on their own people, you know, themselves. I think that is the only occasion that -- I don't remember hearing about any other occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It was precisely what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 5D541, please. This is a Dutch-Bat report dated June 24, 1995, and I would like the next page to be shown, the following page. I'm mainly interested in the bottom part of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You can see the third paragraph from the bottom of the page, and we can read the following: [In English] "We urge you to be very careful about who was responsible for this incident. There is a possibility BiH made up this attack to influence our opinion about the situation in the enclave and to influence public opinion." [Interpretation] So what I would like to know is if the UNMOs or yourself sent a similar report regarding this incident.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, our report indicated that there was a BSA infiltration.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You told us yesterday, on page 47 of the transcript, that you had the list of weapons that Serbs had. Who had given you that list?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't remember saying that we had a list of weapons that the Serbs had. All we had was what we got there as having been used by -- by the Serbs, not necessarily a list of the weapons that the Serbs had, because we never saw them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I will read what you stated on the transcript yesterday. On page 47 of the transcript of yesterday, you said, I quote -- or at least it was written as such: [In English] "We had a list of weapons that they had: Artillery shells, missiles, rocket-launchers, and all that." [Interpretation] I will not spend too much time on this question, but are you telling us today that it was not true, that you never had such a list?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the list here indicates really what they used, not necessarily what they had. What was used is what we found there. And after analysing everything that was -- that was there, we came up with a list of what was used during the attack, and this is what we provided.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you tell us where this list of used weapons or weapons that were used at the time is?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The list is there. I think it is in -- in one of the reports, in the document that you already have. It is there in one of the sitreps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday, on page 21, you told us that you did not know if Muslim authorities of Srebrenica were stopping people from leaving the enclave. Would you be surprised to find out that, in fact, the authorities of Srebrenica were stopping people from leaving?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wouldn't be surprised. In desperation, anyone can do anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown document 5D244, please. It's an order, once again, from the Command of the 28th Division of the 27th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the first paragraph, you can see that the command of all the units of the 28th Division should take all the measures to prevent army members and civilians from leaving the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can read that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Tell us, please, your contacts in Srebrenica, the civilian authorities or military authorities, did they ever tell you that they had problems with people leaving the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Look at paragraph 3. At the beginning of the paragraph, the command of the Division ordered to its units to do -- go about their tasks of combat. It is the 280th, 83rd, and 285th Light Brigade. Can you confirm that you never heard about these brigades?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I never heard of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown page 2 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You can see on this document it's been drafted by Ramiz Becirovic, a person which you knew. Ramiz Becirovic was one of your contact points, with certain information coming from him?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: My question was: Is it true that some information which you obtained came from Ramiz Becirovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I'm lost. What information, because I didn't see that. What information could you be referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that you were three observers and that you had to obtain information from somebody in order to be able to check this information. Is it true that some information, in particular on the Serbian attacks, were given by Ramiz Becirovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true, some of the military issues, you know, issues to do with the enclave. From the beginning, I said we were discussing with Ramiz Becirovic and also with the mayor of the Opstina. So we were in constant touch with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Indeed, both the mayor and Ramiz Becirovic gave you information, the information which suited them?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that I may not -- I may not know. The information we were getting is the information they give us. So whether it's the one that suited them or not, I really cannot -- cannot tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question was in another sense. I think you to understand the question put to you as being the following: Would you accept that in giving you a series of information, Ramiz Becirovic and others may have been taking you down the garden path, feeding you false information on purpose? Would you accept that, that that could have been the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really won't take it that way, because there were many issues that we were discussing concerning the enclave that really you could see that was true, and it's not everything that we were saying that was not correct or that he was telling us or that interested -- was to their interests. But at the same time, I think it's worth remembering that when we have two warring factions, definitely you get from one side what they want you to know and also what they want you to convey to the other side. Likewise, when we go to the other side, the BSA side, they were telling us what they know from their side and what they want us to convey to the BiH. So these are issues that by now maybe, Your Honour, you should see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You spoke of humanitarian aid, and you said that a part of the humanitarian aid brought by UNHCR was sold on the market. Do you know how it was possible that the humanitarian aid was sold on the market, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me start by correcting that. It's not that humanitarian aid brought by UNHCR was sold on the market. It is that part of it was being sold on the market, because the interpretation here may mean that everything that was brought in by the UNHCR was being sold at the market. But the locals sometimes could save a bit of it. You said you see the other part being sold in the market. That was evident. We could see part of it being sold in the market, but not everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Who was monitoring the distribution of humanitarian aid inside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, when there was a distribution of -- of this humanitarian aid, we used to send one observer to go there and see what is happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you inform the UNHCR that part of the humanitarian aid was later on the market, was to be seen on the market?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were also aware. We used to see it, and they were also aware about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And did you -- you did say, sir, a part, a small part, you said, was taken by the BH Army. Did you inform UNHCR of the fact that the BH Army took part of the humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no -- there was nothing like that they were taking this apart in proportion, maybe a certain percentage. But at least even the UNHCR knew about the soldiers, that is, the BiH also being given a bit of the proportion, but not in percentage form that it is official, they've got to get this percentage of what is distributed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown document 5D65. And just before that, it's a report from the Dutch Institute, NIOD. This is just an excerpt of this report. Could you please show page 3 of the document, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you see the last paragraph? You can read the first two sentences: [In English] "In the meantime, the ABiH in Srebrenica appeared to be taking good care of itself. In May, the ABiH separated approximately 40 tons of goods from UNHCR."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I -- .

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those 40 tons, it's a considerable quantity, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, yes. It's quite a considerable quantity, but we were not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But you -- you knew that the Dutch-Bat was searching the convoys of UNHCR before they entered the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware that Dutch-Bat was searching the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like you to see document 5D545, copy books, notebooks which were transmitted to the Prosecution and which we obtained. No, it's not that exhibit or this document. It is the right number in the transcript. Could we see page 12 of the document. Excuse me. Could I see the ERN number of this page. I need to see ERN number 3828, page 12. Apparently, it's a mistake. It should be page 4, apparently. Yes, that's the right page. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You see here you were in a meeting with several people, and towards the lower part of the page, you can see: [In English] "Search by Dutch-Bat on UNHCR convoys should continue." [Interpretation] Do you remember something of that? Does it ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see where you -- where you're reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: While you were looking, you see at a given moment it is the Chief of Staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina who's speaking, "COS BiH," and after that there is a hyphen, and there I repeat what I said because it was not in the transcript: [In English] "Search by Dutch-Bat..." [Microphone not activated] "Search by Dutch-Bat on UNHCR convoys continue."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, do you -- does it help you to remember this topic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what this means, and if you read the whole paragraph in totality, is that this is the Chief of Staff saying it, that -- about the information he had gotten concerning the convoy and that the BSA would get a token, because that is what he's saying he had, and that the search by Dutch-Bat on the UNHCR convoys should continue. That does not necessarily mean that it was actually happening or that I knew about it. I'm writing about what the Chief of Staff was saying, if you can read that paragraph in totality.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I understand that maybe you were not aware of that before this meeting. But if the representative of the BH Army said that the search should continue, that means they were in progress, and they existed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, one may interpret it that way. But as far as I was concerned, there was no such a -- there was no such thing being done by UN -- by Dutch-Bat on UNHCR convoys. I don't -- I don't remember knowing something like that. I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know that Medicins Sans Frontieres was present, the organisation Medicins Sans Frontieres were present in Srebrenica; are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you arrived at Srebrenica in April 1995, you heard that there were problems between the municipal authorities and that organisation?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did. There were problems between them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown an exhibit, 1D470, which we've already shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is a debriefing with your colleague when you arrived in Zagreb on the 24th of July, 1995, and yesterday you told us that you remembered this briefing or debriefing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you had two notebooks. One was destroyed, you destroyed it, and the other one, the one we have seen now, you had it when you arrived in Zagreb, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, I had that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Why -- do you have an explanation why this -- for these briefing notes, at the middle of paragraph two: [In English]" The Kenyan officer seemed to have no written record"?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what is written there, that I seem to not have written records, and it's true. When we were being debriefed, I did not have it. That does not mean I did not have it in my -- in my dwelling area in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could page 5 be shown now, please, page 5 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you see paragraph 23? It's about Sunday and Monday, 9/10 July; and in paragraph 24, you can read: [In English] "The compound in Potocari was not fired on at all; although, it could easily have been." [Interpretation] Is this what you have said to your colleagues in Zagreb on the 24th of July, 1995? Is that what you told them? The question was: Did you and your colleagues, have you said that in Zagreb on the 24th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think this is correct. I don't think we're the ones who said it. I don't know who this report is coming from, because the compound in Potocari was fired at several times. We were reporting that in our sitreps, and we even indicated that even the day we were going in, there was -- there was shelling in the Potocari compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 25, it is a question of Tuesday, therefore, on the 11th of July; and then on the second sentence: [In English] "However, the factory at Potocari was already full and they had to stop 100 metres outside the compound. This was not seen as a problem because it was already noted that the BSA were not firing on the area." [Interpretation] The only question I'm interested in is that effectively, at a given moment on the 11th of July, the refugees could not enter the compound anymore; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true they could not enter. It was already full.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could now page 3 be shown, page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We can see paragraph 13, and this paragraph has been noted: [In English] "There were allegedly no stores of food and the civilian population was getting very unruly because of this. In fact, there were many smuggling routes that brought in food every day. OPK reported 40-50 horses bringing in food each day from Zepa. Occasionally, the BSA ambushed the trail, but it still went on. "There was some payment going on at a high level between the BSA and the BiH to allow this transport. UNMOs were not allowed to see inside the Opstina storage area to check food stocks." [Interpretation] What I'm interested in is the last sentence of this paragraph. Yesterday, you told us that you could go and see the warehouse where the food stuffs were. Perhaps you made a mistake. Is it possible? Is it true that you couldn't go and see the contents of the warehouse, or at least not always?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, at least we could go there and count the food that was inside there. We were able to do that. If maybe there's a day that we could not or one of us was not able to go there, maybe that is an exception, but at least most of the time we were allowed to go there and see what was inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So what you say now is that indeed there were exceptions and that sometimes you were not allowed to enter and see. You leave the possibility that there were situations where you couldn't go in and see?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the possibility I leave is that maybe an observer, once or twice or whatever number, maybe was not allowed; but as far as I know, whenever we wanted to go in there to see what is inside, we were able to, to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You have no explanation why this sentence is in the debriefing report in Zagreb on the 24th of July, three days only after you left the enclave of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said this could have been maybe one instant, but the number of times we wanted to go there --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: All right. Now -- all right, now, this paragraph also speaks of the food which was coming from Zepa. You knew that food stuffs were coming from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we -- I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You also knew that Zepa was an enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Have you ever asked the municipality authorities how it happened that Zepa had enough food to feed also the people in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never asked, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the 13th of December last, you mentioned the British who were in the enclave, and you said that they could go anywhere, and they had a vehicle, a Land Rover in particular. Do you know who was giving, furnishing the petrol to these British personnel so that they could use their vehicle?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not know, but it could have been coming from either UNHCR or Dutch-Bat. That, I'm not aware. I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know who sent these British people inside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who sent them in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you don't know to whom they reported, either?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that on the 9th of July, when you left Srebrenica and went to Potocari, you had a problem, which was to go back to Srebrenica, and you sent your interpreter there to give you some information, to report, to tell you what was going on at Srebrenica. If I understood what you said on the 13th of December, page 19218, it was too dangerous for you - I'm talking about the UNMOs, not you personally - to go back to Srebrenica, to return. Is that a fact?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Your interpreter at the time was only 20 years old, Emir Suljagic. Your interpreter at the time, he was just 20 years old or so?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had just celebrated his 20 -- 20 years, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Didn't you feel that it was also dangerous for your interpreter to return to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is indicated in my report very clearly, that we found us going back to Srebrenica, in our white vehicle, soft-skinned vehicle, and our blue helmets. I think it's very clear in my report that it could have made us a collective target. We could easily have been seen. So after we discussed together, that is, we observers and the interpreter, we agreed he can go there using that route through the river all the way up, because through that he could not be -- he could not be seen. But with us, we couldn't go back to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to see P501.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It's your own report, your report of the 10th of July. What I'm interested in is the second part of this report, where there's this question of the shells of 150 [as interpreted] millimetres. In this report, we read that it was probably shells of 155 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the word "probably" was the word used by your interpreter when he told you what was going on, or was it a word used by the drafter of the report? Was it added by the person who drafted the report, this "probably"?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is our report, and the word "probably" means we were not sure whether it is the 155-millimetre shells or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I understand very well, but was it the interpreter who was on the spot who wasn't sure or was it you who weren't sure of what the interpreter was telling you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is we who are not sure of what he was telling us. We could not confirm that is exactly 155 or any other calibre.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this report, you say nowhere that this information was given by interpreter. Anybody reading this report could think it was one of the UNMOs who had seen that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it is true, one can interpret that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In fact, you should have said that this information was not confirmed by the UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown P1533. This is an aerial photograph of Potocari. Would it be possible to zoom on the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to ask you: On the 12th of July in Potocari, there were a lot of people, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, there were. There were a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And on this photograph, you can see people just in the middle of the road going towards a bus. You don't see people anywhere else. Does this photo correspond to what you saw in Potocari on the 12th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it does. I think it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madame Fauveau, you've already taken an hour and ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask for an extra five minutes, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: How is it that here you can't see any people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Objection to the way the question is phrased, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will go to another topic, and it will be my last question, if I could put my last question. Could the witness be shown Exhibit P515, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is your report, sir, dated 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown paragraph 6. It's at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It talks about the fact that 50 babies were born. Would you agree, sir, that there must be a mistake there and that, in fact, they probably meant five babies and not 50 babies?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, it is possible. I can't remember whether there were five or 50. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I will not spend too much time on this, but I would like to remind you that in your personal journal, you noted that in 1993 a hundred babies were born; and 1994 and 1995, 1.040 babies were born, which on an average brings us to two to three babies a day. So to my mind, "five babies" seems to be a plausible number. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I say, right now I cannot remember whether it was five or 50, so it's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madame Fauveau. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My name is David Josse, and I represent General Gvero. You have described, Colonel Kingori, being very scared as you left Srebrenica on the 9th of July. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you described, with what might be described as a disarming frankness, being very, very scared on the journey to Potocari that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Potocari, you spent a fair amount of your time there in a bunker; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct, Your Honour. Immediately, we entered Potocari, we established a communication -- our communication net, and it is well documented. We have written that. We never entered the bunker immediately we went there. So it's all documented that we started establishing a communication link with our headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I didn't say you spent -- went there immediately. I said you spent a fair amount of your time inside the bunker. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Who else was with you in this bunker?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which bunker are you talking about? In Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever there was firing, we would go into a bunker, and I was not alone. There was many of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is people from Dutch-Bat and ourselves as UN observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've been asked a great deal about your time in the enclave prior to the commencement of hostilities and whether you were aware of any aggression inside the enclave from Muslims or any general military activity on the part of the Muslims; and for the most part, you weren't aware of either aggression or military activity. Is that a fair summary of what you've been saying over the last few days?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, we were not aware of the Muslim military activity. We were not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And, in particular, you've been at pains to point out that you were not aware of any complaint by the VRS of Muslim military activity?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, the journal or the diary that Ms. Fauveau, the counsel who's just been cross-examining you, have taken to you to, you brought to the Hague with you on Tuesday; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you have a read of it prior to giving evidence in December?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had not gone through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you read it on your way to The Hague this week?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It, on a number of occasions, does it not, makes mention of meetings you attended prior to the outbreak of hostilities, in other words, in particular May and in particular June of 1995, where Serbs made clear that they were very unhappy about military activity by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, there was some mention about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why haven't you previously mentioned it, Mr. Kingori, when you've been asked repeatedly on the topic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I remember mentioning that; and especially when I said that when - if you want me to go back to it - when the BSA were complaining mainly about the BiH activities, whenever a deal went sour, that is what we had and it's documented. Whenever there was a disagreement between these two groups when they inhabited the -- or the Muslims were going to Tuzla or any other place to get food and come back, whenever there was a disagreement, that is the only time that the BSA could come and complain about incursions or even presence or passage of the BSA -- the BiH through the Serb-held territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you're saying that you understood this to be some sort of elaborate ploy on the part of the Serb negotiators, where they were making this up in order to in some way subvert these negotiations; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I won't summarise it that way. They had the reasons to say whatever they wanted to say, and so we would not just dismiss it as such. But we had to weigh the situation as it was at that particular moment, given the fact that we were getting information from all sides and from all the groups concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: "We" in this context is who, Colonel? You, the UNMOs, or the UNMOs and Dutch-Bat?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at a few entries, if we may, in this diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't have the advantage of my copy having ERN numbers at the bottom, so this is going to be a little tricky to do. I sought here -- heard the number "5D545." I didn't actually know it was in e-court. Let's see how we get on. The seventh page, at the bottom. No, these pages, unfortunately, don't marry up. Is there an unmarked hard copy? I've, in fact, got one. We've got a bigger one. There are two versions. Thank you, thank you very much. Perhaps you'd give that one to the witness and perhaps you'd put this one on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you have the original with you, Mr. Kingori?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is inside there. I have it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's in the witness room, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps when I continue after the break, if you'd bring it back in with you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, the bit that I want to refer you to is there on the screen in the left-hand side of the page. It's not entirely clear to me when the meeting you are referring to took place. You might be able to help with that, but we can see --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, other side of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It says: "BSA said the enclave is not fully demilitarised. All inferences to and from the enclave will be closed as of today. BiH are seen at UNPROFOR Ops, and BSA will shoot them. The situation should go back to normal soonest." Then it's clear from the next comment that the commander of Dutch-Bat was present at the meeting. Now, presumably this was some sort of meeting and you were taking minutes. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I was taking my own minutes so that I can convey the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I might just ask if we could go back a couple of pages, because I'm -- I'm not sure that, if we just look at what this memorialises, that this actually memorialises a meeting in which the witness was present with the BSA. I don't mean any disrespect to my friend; but just to make the record clearer, if we go back to the preceding page, it refers to a meeting with Dutch-Bat, UNMOs, and the BiH, in which they relate a meeting between the liaison team from Dutch-Bat and the BSA. I just wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You heard what Mr. Thayer just said there, Colonel. That is probably right, isn't it? In other words, this was a meeting between Dutch-Bat and Muslim authorities, in which they were relaying allegations that the Serbs were making? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, maybe you can let me go back to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to the other pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But the reason, frankly, I'm not very concerned about that, is that what I'm trying to elicit is the fact that you were made aware of allegations that the VRS were making. Whether they're making it to you or making it indirectly, you knew about it, didn't you? That's the thrust of the questions I'm about to ask you. I want you to be clear about that.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I'm lost. Maybe you'll bring me back on track, because I don't get what question actually -- your actual question. You read these and I have read it, but I don't get the actual question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The question is: This is an occasion when you were being made aware that the Serbs were complaining about Muslim military aggression; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that they were talking about the military activities that was not fully -- according to them, it was not at that time demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's go forward a few pages, the 4th of June, because it's a little bit clearer. So at the left-hand side of my page, it says: "4th of June, 1995, meeting with the BiH, Dutch-Bat," and someone called Mr. Ramisi [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I think Madam Usher is not in a position to follow. Do you have some kind of other identification reference? Okay. She found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, unfortunately, it's not that. It's two pages on from that, two pages on. It is that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, it does appear that at this meeting, no Serb was present. But here we see that the BSA have threatened to shoot at BiH soldiers using..." is that "artillery"? Is that short for "artillery"?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Artillery," that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: "... or other weapons if the BiH keep shooting at BSA from UN positions. The BSA have ensured the enclave that unarmed civilians will be saved and they will attack only armed soldiers." Colonel, you were aware, weren't you, that the VRS were suggesting that the Muslims were acting in an aggressive manner towards them?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the issue was in here. Whenever we had meetings with the BSA, whatever they told us we conveyed to the BiH, and vice versa. So you can see here now this is we are reporting what we have been told to the BiH. We are telling them that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- what the BSA are saying. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is why today you continued telling this Trial Chamber that you weren't aware of these allegations. That's been the thrust of your evidence today and before Christmas. Why?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that these reports were being made, you know, we got to look at the whole issue in totality, in that the threats that we were getting, the reports that we were getting from the BSA concerning what was happening inside the enclave or even outside, there's the Muslims who were getting out to Zepa or any other place, this is actually what is written here. These are accurate reports we were getting from them. When we are telling the Muslims, we are telling them so that they can also tell us whether it is true, verify if it is true that that is actually happening, because we've got to tell them, and I never say they never did that. In one of my reports, and I think in my statement, I indicated that we were being told that the Muslims were actually infiltrating on the -- on the Serb side. In fact, they were going to Zepa, and that is indicated. And there were activities, and especially when there were problems between the two -- between the two groups. That is all indicated, so I'm not hiding anything out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: On the 13th of December, you were asked whether Major Nikolic or Colonel Vukovic or any other Serb - and I'm paraphrasing here at page 19168 - ever complained that Muslim forces were attacking from inside the enclave or outside the enclave. You give quite a long answer, and you end by saying: "It was, I think, very rare or never occurred."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That answer is correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Then would you explain why this diary is peppered with references to allegations that Serbs have made to the contrary?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the whole document, how many meetings did we have with the BSA? How many meetings did we have with the BiH? If you look at all that, you'll find that the complaints about the -- the incursions by the -- by the BiH actually are minimal, very few, if any, and I still stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were at pains, weren't you, in December to tell the Trial Chamber about the allegations that you say -- or, I beg your pardon, about what Colonel Vukovic said as to how he was going to have all the Muslims removed from the enclave or forced out of the enclave. You obviously remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why is it not in the diary?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not everything that happened is in this diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You mentioned Colonel Vukovic in the diary on at least two places, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but it's not necessarily the meeting that he said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No. So it's -- why is it not recorded in the diary? Explain to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've just said that it's not everything that is recorded in this -- in this diary, and I said from the beginning that there were -- there was another diary and also there was no limitation on the number of books that you could go out with. Maybe it was in another book that I destroyed, but the issue is that was reported even in our daily sitrep. It is official. He said it and I recorded it, so the issue of the diary does not arise in this case. The point is what we were reporting to the UN system is that that is what Colonel Vukovic said. It is evidence, and I remember very well I was in that meeting and he said it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we need to stop here, Mr. Josse. We'll continue at 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, one moment, because I'm not worried about ourselves and you having lunch because we can always find something to eat, but what about the accused? I would like to know, and I want to be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to speak these fellows, who can speak for themselves, but I know food is provided on a daily basis. Whether it amounts to lunch is another issue, but certainly they are provided with food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but what I mean is that they are not going back to the Detention Unit and come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But of course not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what I wanted to ensure is that they are given something to eat while they are here and that they are not kept --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, as I tried, obviously not very effectively, to explain, is that they are provided with a packed lunch. They have a packed lunch, and I think they're all satisfied. Perhaps I apologise to any one of them if they're not happy with what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll meet in 30 minutes' time from now, thank you. Yes, 20 past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a quick question to Mr. Josse. What we have in e-court is not a full pact, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This diary?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think it is the full pact, as I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Twenty-seven pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, I think, can help more on that, much more than me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just to add a little bit of detail, I advised my friends in an e-mail that there were numerous blank pages throughout the diary, two big chunks of blank pages where the diary - pardon me, I'm a little under the weather - where the diary basically stopped at a particular date. We did not scan those blank pages, given the press of time to get it into the hands of my friends, but the original has been available for their review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At any rate, for future reference, I would like to know the e-court pages later on, in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I'm going to come back to that document in a moment, and I have marked in red, on the copy I had, the passages that I'm going to go to, to make life for all of us easier. I regret to say that in a few moments' time, I'm going to show the witness some other documents which also aren't in e-court, but I think they will be less problematical.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kingori, when we broke off, I was asking you about your allegation as to what Vukovic had said to you about expelling and killing Muslims, and you had told the Trial Chamber that it wasn't in your diary, that it didn't matter, because it was in your daily sitrep. You're sure about that, are you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am. The official documents of the UN is the sitrep, and we ensured that we put it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw the relevant sitrep, the one that had that report of the conversation with Vukovic in?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in -- the last time, I think, it was in December. At least I saw it at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's have a look at another document which might shed some light on that very topic, and it's part of the NIOD report. Now, you were asked about the NIOD report earlier by Ms. Fauveau. Do you know what it is? There's no reason why you should know what it is; but if you don't, I think I should tell you so -- out of fairness, because I'm actually going to put a number of passages from it to you.
