Do you know what the NIOD report is?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: NIOD, I don't understand what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What it is is it's a report, and it was prepared I think at the behest of the Dutch government by an independent institute which investigated, in great depth, the events surrounding the fall of Srebrenica and the events subsequent to the fall of the enclave. Okay?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, I understand now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And parts of it have been referred to in passing in the course of this case, and I think you'll answer my next question. It makes a number of passing references to you, in your role. You obviously weren't aware of that. Since you didn't know what the NIOD report is, you presumably didn't know what it said about you; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true, I don't know about it. I don't know what it said about me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to have a look at this part, first of all, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This needs to go on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, to help, what's going on the ELMO is a small section of part 3 of this very long report called "The Fall of Srebrenica," chapter 4: "The Mood in the Enclave, May-July 1995". That heading has in effect been cut-and-pasted into this bit, and this bit, itself, comes from section 7. So we all know what we're talking about. I'm going to read aloud, in fact, the first two paragraphs here. It says this: "With respect to the opening of a corridor for the population, UNMO Major Joseph Kingori stated in 1997 that he had been invited in early June by VRS Major Nikolic to a meeting in Hotel Fontana in Bratunac, which was also attended by VRS Colonel Vukovic, as well as another high-ranking VRS officer. "The VRS delegation had taken this opportunity to state through Vukovic that the entire population would have to leave the enclave. In addition, Vukovic is said to have threatened that if this did not happen, he would have the population killed. However, if the population were to leave, they would be offered safe passage to Tuzla. "Kingori understandably said that the meeting had left him with the feeling that something was in the air if no use were to be made of the corridor. He also assumed that the Bosnian Serbs had passed on the same message to the UN headquarters, but no indications can be found for this in the UNPROFOR archives. The message clearly did not reach this destination." Do you understand what the author of the report is trying to say there, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's in complete variance to what you told the Chamber before the adjournment we've just had, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily, because when we wrote the report and we sent it to the UN headquarters, whether someone could have found it later or not, really, we may not know. I may not know. But the point is he said that, we recorded it, and we sent it to the UN headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. Could we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The paragraph I'm leaving out, in fact, simply deals with your testimony here in the Krstic trial. The next page, which is the paragraph after the one I've left out, reads as follows: "What is surprising is that Kingori had apparently not reported back what was discussed so that it could reach Dutch-Bat." That, you're saying, is inaccurate. Is that correct, Major -- Colonel, I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What they're saying is what is surprising is that Kingori had apparently not reported back what was discussed so that it could reach Dutch-Bat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you tell Dutch-Bat what Vukovic had said to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we told them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So what this sentence that I have just read out states is inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's go on: "Neither was the subject raised at the debriefing of the UNMOs, including Kingori, after the fall of Srebrenica." It's not in your debriefing, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not asked that question, and so I don't remember whether we raised it -- we raised it ourselves or not. But at least this was known by everybody in the UN headquarters. They knew about what we had reported about Colonel Vukovic, about the threats he had made. Right now I think I can remember very well we talked about it during the debrief. We talked about it. We told them about what they -- the events that happened just prior to the fall of the enclave. We talked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I think we can rest assured, Colonel, that if what this report says is inaccurate, when Mr. Thayer asks some questions a little later, he'll put us right. I mean, it may be the report is wrong and you're right, but we'll no doubt discover shortly. So I'll move on, if I may. Let's go back, if we may, to your journal. I'll call it that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document I've just referred to, perhaps that needs a number. I don't know if I can have some assistance from Madam Registrar in that regard. No, I need to do that. We'll sort it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next passage I would like to show you is this one marked "number 1".

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To assist, as I say, the marking "number 1" is by me. The marking in the left-hand margin on the left of the "1" was not by me, could I emphasise to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This relates, to save everyone flipping through the diary, to a meeting you had with Dutch-Bat, UNMOs, BiH, and Mr. Ramisi seems to be present again; and, again, I accept that it appears that the Serbs were not at the meeting. So this must be a repeat of what they had said to someone, presumably the Dutch, at an earlier stage. I think this meeting was on the 16th of June. I beg your pardon, it wasn't Mr. Ramisi. It was the Chief of Staff, Mekrem [phoen], a Dutch-Bat liaison officer. This says: "BiH CRS say they have recently requested for assistance from the 2nd Corps HQ and have recently received. He said he feels stronger than he was 15 days ago." Military build-up by the Muslims is what is being said there; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. You can interpret it that way, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, did you interpret it that way? You were at the meeting, you wrote this down.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. Beside that, meeting on the 20th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So number 2, please. This refers to, as I've already said, the 20th of June. If we go down a little bit, we can actually see -- scroll down the page down a little bit. A bit more, please. No, down, on the ELMO to you, yes. No, the other way, the other way. That's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So I won't read out what it says at the top there: "Afternoon, BiH soldiers shot at a BSA vehicle travelling a wrong road to former OPE, and it landed into the river, and a firefight ensued." It looks like there was some ABiH aggression there, doesn't it, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it can be seen it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I repeat my earlier question. Why haven't you mentioned this in your evidence hitherto, after you didn't think it was relevant? Tell the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have mentioned about these incursions. It's only that I may not have mentioned as many times as maybe you think should have been mentioned. But at least I've mentioned somewhere that there were issues to do with the BiH activity inside and even to the BSA on the other side, against the BSA. It is mentioned somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. Could we go to number 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That, again, to put it into context, relates to a meeting on the 27th of June with the BiH, Mr. Ramisi, liaison officer team, UNMO, and here we see it says: "Dutch-Bat protested the armed soldiers along the streets of the enclave." Now, did you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not a matter of even seeing, because I wrote about this even in our sitrep, about the presence of armed soldiers and that we were not happy about it. We saw I think there were three or four along -- along the streets, and we mentioned about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Three or four soldiers, that's all?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, we saw soldiers on the way. I can't remember the actual -- the actual number, but we reported on the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And to waste no time, let's go to number 4, please, which is a meeting of the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You might be able to help here: "Dutch-Bat said the patrol was a normal one and saw five BiH and" and what does the next abbreviation stand for?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 2MG machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: SA?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Small arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: "And carried on with their ..."?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Patrol."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: "... towards 399." What's that a reference to?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 399, that is a trick point, one high ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So, help. Who had the machine-guns and the small arms?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the BiH soldiers that the Dutch-Bat saw. This is a report from Dutch-Bat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: "As they proceeded, they met five BiH soldiers in firing positions who stopped them. The patrol wanted to continue, but 12 other BiH approached from height 789 and loaded them weapons, threatening the Dutch-Bat patrol." Do you --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, this is a report by Dutch-Bat. They are the ones who are briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. And do you recall that being mentioned at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you put that in your sitrep?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You did?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. So you'd agree with me that you were aware of a number of allegations of Muslim aggression prior to the attack on the enclave by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We need to separate some of this. Like, when we are talking about this particular one, the one in front of us right now, this was a complaint by Dutch-Bat itself, not that they were acting against the BSA. Of course, they are armed; and when they are armed, obviously that is an issue to us. But this is Dutch-Bat complaining, not the BSA, because they were now preventing the Dutch-Bat from their routine from carrying on with their duties. The other areas, if you can remember what I said concerning the -- the number of people who were armed inside the enclave as compared to the BSA, you'll find that this is a negligible number, for sure. This is quite negligible. And if you also compare the kind of weapons these people had, five soldiers with two machine-guns and small arms, compared with the ammunition that the BSA had, and you -- and they were around the enclave, it's simply incomparable.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why is that relevant? You've chosen to tell the Trial Chamber those last two sentences. Explain why that's at all relevant to what I've just been asking you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying here is it is important to report everything, and we were reporting everything as we were seeing it. But then you cannot fail to compare the kind of -- the armament or the kind of weapons that the two sides had. You see that this is -- the difference is quite big. The BSA were all around the enclave, fully, fully, fully armed, compared with five -- well, five -- two machine-guns and some small arms. It's quite incomparable, totally incomparable.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll tell you, Colonel, why it's relevant. It's relevant, is it not, because in your mind, you had taken the side of the Muslims and you were not acting in an impartial manner. That's why what you've just said is relevant, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I never said and I never used the word "irrelevant." There's nothing which is irrelevant to a military observer. We, as military observers, we make sure that we report everything that we see, everything that we find, everything that we are told, and we go through all that before we pass it on to the higher headquarters. Secondly, an issue of being biased, as far as I'm concerned, does not arise at all, because I was there as a neutral person. I personally did not have any interests, I never have, and I don't think I will ever have. My country, Kenya, has got no national interest there. What I'm saying is -- I mean national interests that maybe I could be protecting, none at all. So there's no issue of being biased, and there's no reason for me to get biased because that was influencing me or even my judgement at that particular moment concerning what was going on inside the enclave. It's only that you have to compare the two areas, because that was part of our role, so that you can see both sides were unequal. That is true. So there should be no match. The Srebrenica -- the Muslims who were inside there were no match for the Serbs. That's why we were there, to make sure that these guys were safe, because most of the weapons were held somewhere in a safe place, as far as we knew. So comparing this kind of weapons with the other side, that may repeat what I've said, but it is imperative that we realise that there was no reason why an observer like me would be biased at all. There was nothing to force me to get biased to any of the warring factions. I could sit with either side. We could discuss issues. I could report what I was told from this side to the other side. It is on record that even General Ratko Mladic mentioned that he had heard much about us, as observers, and how neutral we were and how good we were to his people. Major Nikolic was also aware that whatever we were reporting, we were very neutral. So there was no doubts about my personal neutrality, and I was not biased at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll move --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Josse. Can I interrupt. If I can put it this way, Mr. Kingori, you just compared the quality of arms that were held by BSA, on the one hand, and those held by the Muslims inside the enclave, on the other hand. But inside the enclave, one was not supposed to be armed at all; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're correct, they're not supposed to be armed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But if you are to compare the quality of arms, you have to compare that of the BSA and that held by the Tuzla or 2nd Corps or whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe it's not very clear, but the -- the reason why one has got to compare is not that you are going there to compare, that is not the aim. The aim is not to compare. The aim is to show that these people inside the enclave were disarmed. And when you notice one or two guns, really, yeah, you're going to report on it, but it's not as much as held on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So my point was that if one is not to be supposed armed at all, then comparison is not relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is true, but I've said that the aim was not to compare. It's only that you are forced, when you see the kind of reaction from the other side and this other side, because at the same time, because the enclave was demilitarised, the BSA were not supposed to harm or even fire at the enclave, but they were also doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You, in your evidence in December, described, I think in graphic detail, the attack on the enclave, and you used, on a number of occasions, the word "onslaught," and I suppose you don't resile from a strong word like that, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Onslaught."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That was a word you chose to use on at least two occasions before Christmas.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, I may have used it. I don't remember very well, but I may have used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I want to summarise your description of this onslaught. On the 6th of July, you said that you heard about 250 ordinance; 7th, 250; the 8th, you said, was the heaviest day. I don't think you gave a figure, but clearly it was more than 250; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The 9th, you said you heard over 100, and of course you moved to Potocari. And on the 10th, you again heard shells from Potocari. You said 100, plus other detonations; and, of course, you were also getting information from Emir, your yellow card. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So we are talking about something like a thousand shells, are we, falling on Srebrenica in this period?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, around that figure, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And that's a lot of shells, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you go to Srebrenica after these events? In other words, when you left Potocari, you didn't go back to Srebrenica, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You did?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you went back and you saw what damage these thousand shells had caused?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the shelling was not just inside the village of Srebrenica. It was not just in the town. Where I went was the town, and I saw the kind of damage that was inside there, not necessarily caused by the 1.000 shells, because the 1.000 shells were not on the Srebrenica town as the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, because a good number of these shells were targeted at surrounding hills, where there were Muslim military encampments; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were just missing their targets and hitting the hills, and that is mentioned also.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were there Muslim military encampments in the hills, fighters?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Before I go on with this, did you go to Vukovar after it had been shelled? Were you in Vukovar at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukovar, yeah. That was my first station en route.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. And were you there after it had been shelled by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's when I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What state was it in?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: A state of disrepair.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. It was very badly damage?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, you are quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Compare Vukovar to the village of Srebrenica after it had been shelled by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's good to compare that, but I don't know whether you know that the kind of damage that was in Vukovar was caused by different things. I mean, it was not just shelling from outside. Vukovar, what those people did, they were going into houses and putting mines or detonations and then detonating the whole building. This is different from mass shelling from the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Answer the question. You said it was good to compare it. Compare it, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness is trying to answer the question and, in fact, did answer the question. I think my friend needs to just calm down a little bit and keep the temperature a little lower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we send him outside on the terrace? Yes, I think you can safely move to the next question, Mr. Josse. I mean, he's told you that he cannot really draw a comparison because the circumstances would have --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll go back to Srebrenica, Mr. Thayer will be relieved to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me then ask you: You went there. Describe the damage that you saw in Srebrenica after all these days of shelling.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Srebrenica was not the same anymore. It was not the same place that we had left. A lot of buildings had been freshly damaged, part of the roads were cratered, also the Bravo Company compound had also been cratered, and a lot of other areas. The PTT building had also been hit, and all those other damages. The place was very different. It was not the PTT. It was not the Srebrenica that we had left, I think, three or four or five days earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was going to ask you to specify which building you say had been hit. You say the PTT was hit. Any others, significant buildings that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hospital had also been hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: By a shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the actual location, but it was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's have a look.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we reported that also.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at 6D209, please. Your Honour, this is a still from a video of the 14th of July, part of the trial video.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's the hospital, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember it very well now. It's all those years ago, but at least I can see it. It could be a hospital, itself, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Where was that building hit, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember which place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 6D214, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is that the PTT?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recognise it from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Does that help you at all? PTT?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, I'm told that's the police station. I'm sorry, my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which one, this one or the previous?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This one, this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you recognise it, Colonel, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This one, I don't. I don't recognize it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at 6D210, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not a great picture, I concede, but that's a bit of a Bravo compound; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be. It's not very clear, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I certainly wouldn't trust you with mounting a photography exhibition, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I concede that. Perhaps I should have played the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Anyway, your recollection is of damage in the way that you've described to the PTT, the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, the Bravo Company compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just ask you this: Mr. Lazarevic showed you the mortar being fired earlier from the petrol station. What distance is that petrol station from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I remember? Really, I cannot. I can't be able to estimate now for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Presumably, you can't remember what distance it was from the PTT either.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I can't. I can't. I can't visualise where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you went back, what state was the mosque in?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the mosque. I didn't go to the mosque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the evidence in the case has shown that there is more than one mosque in Srebrenica, so if my friend could be a little more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is one in town, downtown, and one as you enter, before you enter Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It wasn't designed as a trick question. The witness could have told us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you recall there was more than one mosque, without being reminded?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, at least I know there are mosques inside the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm suggesting to you that you're exaggerating this damage. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand what you are saying, but I don't agree with it, because the damage, I saw to it, and it was different from the way it was before. After all that shelling, definitely it was different. I saw it. And though I did not go throughout the whole village, at least where I saw, I could see there was a lot of damage, as compared to how it was when we were there before we left for Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you surprised it wasn't more damage, bearing in mind the extent of the shelling that you have described?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So it was lucky, Srebrenica, in your estimation?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my estimation, it was lucky.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you've already said that you take the same view as to the number of wounded and fatalities. It was surprising there were so few, bearing in mind the ferocity of the attack?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So coincidence favoured the inhabitants on this occasion? "Good fortune," perhaps I should have said.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On what? I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll move on. I've asked that question. Now, I said I was going to come back to the NIOD report. I want to take you to another part of it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I might have a moment. I think it may be on the ELMO. I hope so. No, it's not, it's bare. I beg your pardon. Again, Madam Usher, you're going to have to stand by the ELMO. My apologies, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We've got part 4, the repercussion and the aftermath until the end of 1995. This is part of Chapter 4: "Potocari-Dutch-Bat and the fate of the local population." This is section 24 which deals with observations and reports by the UNMOs. You might want to read that first page perhaps to yourself so that you are fully aware of what knowledge the author of this report gained about your role, in effect. Whilst you are doing that, to summarise, the first paragraph really deals with the role of UNMO in general, and the second paragraph specifically deals with UNMO involvement in the events in Srebrenica, and explains what should have happened, at least in theory. When you finish, say so.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I've read.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to read the next paragraph and ask you some questions: "The reality of the UNMO activities during the last days of Srebrenica was rather less rosy. When the attack began, there were three UNMOs in the enclave." That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: "Three others had left on June 24th to be rotated, but the VRS did not allow their replacements to enter the enclave." You've told us about that already, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: "Many Dutch soldiers, including the battalion's commanding officers, later criticised the three remaining UNMOs in Srebrenica." Are you now aware, Colonel, that you have been criticised by Dutch-Bat in the way that this report describes, or was this the first time you've learnt of it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the -- the first time I'm learning about it, but we could also criticise them. They failed in very many areas. They are the ones who failed the enclave. So it's not a matter of them criticising us. We were doing our job, and we did it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's go on: "They complain," this is Dutch-Bat, "about their," that is UNMO's "'invisibility,' tendency to hold back, and even fear in monitoring and reporting the events during the crucial days of the fall of the enclave and what happened afterwards." What do you say about that allegation that Dutch-Bat, certain members of it, has made against you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is very inaccurate. In actual fact, we were the main force in the enclave, and they were even depending on us to escort them. We were the ones who were monitoring the whole enclave, when these guys had gone back to the battalion headquarters. In fact, we were left out there to monitor whatever activities were happening. And even in some of the reports somewhere, I've written that we were left alone and we were in soft-skinned vehicles, and we were patrolling the enclave alone. And in fact, at that time, we were just two, not three, because that one, a Dutch, was already in Dutch-Bat compound. In fact, when the shelling started, and even about a week before that, we were only two military observers, me and Major David Tetteh. The other one, Dehan, was in the Dutch-Bat compound. So considering the actual situation at that time, you can see we were doing our work, and we were monitored. We were everywhere. It's only that we were limited by the number that we had, two. In fact, we did not even form a patrol. A patrol team was supposed to be two and one interpreter, and that is one; and then you get another two and an interpreter together. You move out together. But here, we ourselves were separating. We were leaving one observer in the offices, and we could put one observer in the vehicle, and an interpreter, to form like a team. Does that mean cowardice or fear? You going out there, knowing that you are alone as an observer. We were patrolling and coming back and giving reports, even during the fighting. When the shelling was continuing, we were going out there. We could leave one person inside the office, and we go out. So what they are saying here, this is not true at all. Maybe they're just trying to justify their own failures. As far as I'm concerned, we did our job to the best of our ability, considering the limitations that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to go through other parts of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For how much longer?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to go through the rest of this page, Your Honour. But, I mean, the witness gave a very long answer. I'm not going to stop him. If the Chamber feels that the answers are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But how much more time do you require, because you have exceeded the one hour already.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd say 15 minutes to go through the rest of this page, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's make it ten, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll go on: "Karremans," who was the commander, "as well as Franken," who was his deputy, "accused the UNMOs of not taking greater advantage of their special position and wider mandate to at least try to follow the events better." What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is all false.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: "In Karremans' eyes, they could have followed convoys by car; or at the start of the evacuation, they can stand in the middle of Bratunac, so to speak. Moreover, the UNMOs would even have been able to use the excuse that their second office was in Bratunac, at the Hotel Fontana." What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a flat lie. It is a flat lie, and I don't know. Whoever was writing this, whoever gave this, really was just trying to justify his position by discrediting others or he was under pressure. This is someone who was under pressure somewhere, because UNMOs were all the time in their area of responsibility. When we were not, after we left Srebrenica and we went to Dutch-Bat, in fact, we were scattered in the whole of that area to cover the whole -- the whole place. And even when there were meetings, we would go to those meetings. And in fact, calling Bratunac our second office, that is an insult. It is an insult, because Bratunac, we went there I think only twice for meetings which had been requested by the BSA. So this is someone who is trying to, I think, divert attention from their own failures. Karremans failed. That is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, it goes on, in fairness to the report, to say that: "Conversely, the UNMOs complained especially about the poor information that they received from the battalion, something that is supposed to have hampered their activities. Even early on July 12, they already reported their frustration about having been ignored in consultations between Dutch-Bat and other aid organisations. "'They tell us outright we are not required. We feel frustrated.'" However, that may already have been the result of a loss of credibility at the time. Dutch-Bat personnel, as well as local staff, complained about the fact that the UNMOs made their own job more difficult by leaving their office at the post office in Srebrenica quite early in the piece, on July the 9th." In other words, they're suggesting you ran rather too early. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not right. We never ran from our headquarters, and we were giving constant information to the UN headquarters concerning the state of the enclave and about the enclosure -- I mean, the encroachment of the enclave by the tanks from the BSA. And when they were within range of our PTT building, about two kilometres or so, that is the time we decided to leave. By that time, it was very risky to continue staying there, and especially when these are a tank which can get a direct hit. That is not something to joke around with. So we feared for our safety, and it is on record. It is recorded that we decided to request that we be allowed to leave our PTT building. We requested the UN, through the normal UNMO channels, and they agreed that according to the circumstances at that time, we can leave. That is not fear, that is not running away. That is actually going to a safer place. And even after that, the BiH prevented us from leaving, but we requested them further, and it is on record also that later is the time they agreed to let us leave. By that time, the tanks were very close, less than two kilometres away. So do you stay there until you're hit, and people start praising you for having been killed? No, we could not do that. So we decided that our safe bet was to go to the Dutch-Bat compound, which, to us, was slightly safer. And by the way, when saying that we were scared and they were not, how many OPs had been closed at that time? Why did they run away from the BSA?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, the author of this report doesn't, sadly, agree with you, because it goes on to say that: "At the time the UNMOs left Srebrenica in a great hurry, one of them, De Haan, was already in the compound at Potocari," and you've told us that. So moving on a few lines: "The remaining UNMOs, Kingori and Tetteh, already joined him on July the 9th, when things got too hot for them and they left the compound again only after the fall of the enclave." Would you agree with that characterisation, that you left when things got, quote "too hot" for you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. That is exactly what I mean, but also look at where they say that they left the compound again only after the fall of the enclave. Is that true, even to yourself? Did you read the report, that I went back to Srebrenica itself, that I was out -- we were outside the compound, talking to the BSA, monitoring what was happening out there? So what do they mean by inside, that we just stayed inside? This is a distortion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It then goes on and says that it didn't make a very good impression that you sent your yellow card back, and then the last sentence on this page says: "Some Dutch-Bat soldiers like to call the UNMOs 'UNBOs,' standing for 'UN Bunker Observers,' because 'when something had to be observed, these people were sitting in the bunkers.'". You were scared, and the Dutch-Bat characterisation of you, as someone sitting in a bunker is accurate, sadly, isn't it, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a distortion of the truth. This is actually directly the opposite of what we did. We were able to go around the whole enclave. And even during this, this incursion, we were able to monitor what was happening. We reported, and it's evidenced by the reports that we made, the counting of those shells. Going out to analyse, does that mean staying in the bunker? Do you analyse when you are in a bunker? It is in the report that we analysed the craters, did the reports, grid references, and all that. You are not doing that inside the bunker. So I'm sure you also do not believe what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not more than 30 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Cross-examination by Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Colonel, as you know, my name is John Ostojic, and I represent the Mr. Ljubisa Beara. Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want confirm a couple of things from reading your reports or your report of 1997 and your testimony here, sir. Can you confirm to me that you never met Mr. Ljubisa Beara during July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't remember meeting someone of that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So can you confirm that you never heard of his name during the period of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that name is not familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sir, in your September 1997 report that you reviewed prior to giving your testimony in December of last year, can you confirm that you also never mentioned Mr. Ljubisa Beara in that report during the interview that you gave to the Prosecutor from the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not familiar with that. I don't remember that name at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And one last question with respect to specifically Mr. Beara. Can you confirm in the diary that you brought with you this past Tuesday that nowhere in that report do you reference or mention the name of Mr. Beara; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I don't. I have not mentioned him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you a couple questions about these three colonels that you mentioned in your statement and some of which is in your diary. That would be Colonel Vukovic; Colonel Drcic, D-R-C-I-C, as you've identified him in your sit reports and in your statement of 1997; and a Colonel Acamovic. Do you remember those three colonels?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in the interests of time, sir, if I can just -- or if you can help me understand this, you saw and met Colonel Acamovic around July 12th and 13th, 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And did you see him at any time after the 13th of July, 19 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the actual date, but at least he was there, and I don't -- I don't know. I don't know. I can't remember whether I met him after that, really, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can you describe for Your Honours what this colonel looked like? Was he an older man, younger man, middle-aged? Given that he's a Colonel, would you assume that maybe he was in his 50s?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, of course, all colonels are in their 50s. I am one. But he was like -- he was a bit older.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tall or short, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Acamovic, I think this is someone I really cannot be able to describe properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about grey hair? Do you remember the colour of his hair; grey, black, blonde?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't. It's out of my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And other characteristics such as eyeglasses? Do you remember whether he wore any eyeglasses?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't right on this. It's blank.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's talk about the other colonel, D-R-C-I-C, as you've spelled his name before and as reflected in your report. This Colonel Drcic, do you remember what he looked like? Was he taller or shorter than yourself, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drcic. You know, the two, I normally confuse them, Colonel Drcic and Colonel Acamovic. I normally confuse them because I didn't have a lot of interaction with them, not very much. But I can't remember which one was slightly taller than me. There was one that was slightly taller than me and the other one shorter, but I can't remember which one. Drcic, I think, is also in my report, but I would not be able to describe him. I cannot remember him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But do you recall if he had grey hair, sir, or the colour of his hair at all?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall if he had any other distinguishing characteristics, such as eyeglasses or a balding or receding hairline?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, you were one of the military observers. These meetings that you had with Colonel Vukovic -- I'm sorry, with General Acamovic and Colonel Vukovic, they were rather important, were they not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The what?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The meetings that you had or when you met them, those were important encounters, were they not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were. They were important in contrast.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you don't describe them at all in your statement of 1997, and you don't describe them at all in your sit reports; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have described Acamovic, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In terms of physical description, I am asking think, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I described Acamovic; but Drcic, I would not be able to describe him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How about the third colonel, which is Colonel Vukovic, can you describe him better for you than what you have in your statement of September 1997?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Acamovic [sic], I can remember very well. I think he was slightly , not very at all, slightly taller than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you. I'm actually talking about Colonel Vukovic now. I thought we already covered Acamovic. Just so the record is clear, you started by saying that you remember Acamovic very well, and I just want to make sure I'm correct on this.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said Vukovic, not Acamovic. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just on line 5, it says"Acamovic," that is why I reference it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's a mistake. I really wasn't following the transcript, but I heard him distinctly mention --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's why I pointed out just the word clearly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vukovic, I would be able to describe him. As I said, I saw him, I can remember him, and he was slightly taller than me. At that time, I was giving him the age of 50. But when I reached 50, I think he looked slightly older than me. So he was round-faced, sort of, and I think he had a mark somewhere. I can't remember very well. He was very forceful when talking. When he's talking to you, he's a bit forceful.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you remember if he had grey hair or not, sir, or a receding hairline?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hair, no. I just remember the face. The hair, I can't remember how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you say it was a round, large face that you remember for Colonel Vukovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. He was slightly round, round-faced.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me also ask you, if you remember, during the September 1997 interview, you recall that you were at a meeting with a person by the name of "Miroslav Drnic" [phoen]. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in that meeting, there were two colonels present, were there not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And can you tell me, sir, to the best of your recollection, who those two colonels were?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not very sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just quickly, if I read to you from your September 1997 report, on page 12, you reference Colonel Drcic and Colonel Vukovic. Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. Those two could have been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If we look at your sit report, which was an attachment to your September 1997 report, Attachment, I think, number 26, it references those two colonels; correct? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it references the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. One last area, if I may, just to cover with you: When we discussed, sir, in your testimony previously the willingness of the Bosnian Muslims to leave the enclave, you used terms such as "refugees," "displaced persons," et cetera. Do you remember that, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, generally, I used those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, do you recall, sir, in one of your sit reports dated the 8th of July, 1995, that you give a breakdown of the number of inhabitants in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. We give that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And as you sit here, do you remember why you called the people within Srebrenica in July of 1995 as refugees or displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the words were used correctly. I don't know whether it was correct or not, but most of the people inside the enclave were not living in their own natural habitats. Some of them were moved from areas that they were living in before to other areas. A good example would be the [indiscernible] village, where people have built some houses and were taken there. Those are not their normal habitats. That's not where they were living before, so that is why I mentioned, I used those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And when you say "most," sir, would I be correct to interpret that to be 80 to 85 per cent were actually people who were displaced into Srebrenica in July or immediately prior to that of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the type of background that is not with me at the moment, whether they were actually there from the outside or whether they were actually in or displaced or taken to different areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, how do you -- what is your definition of the word "locals"? If people were locals, would that indicate that they were people that were actually from the very area upon which we're discussing?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Locals," it depends on the perspective you are saying it, because if like when we are here, the locals are the people who belong here, but it can be these -- this town, this building, it can be. So for that, I don't remember what --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. What percentage of the Srebrenica population, in July of 1995, were locals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel, if you know, you know. If you don't know, tell us you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 493, please, which is your UNMO report dated the 8th of July, 1995, which was attachment number 1 to your statement in September of 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you remember that report, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I remember this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And just looking on the subject, it talks about the food situation in Srebrenica and the status for food to the civilian population. Immediately below that, under number 1, it talks about the number and status of inhabitants. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And under B, I mean, there is subsection (a), but under (b) you talk about 85 per cent of the people who are there are refugees or displaced persons; and under (c), you say 20 per cent as being locals. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would that be accurate, to be your knowledge, that this an UNMO --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just to make sure we are be accurate, 85 and 20 is a little more than 100 per cent, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that's the percentage, but that could have been, you know, a typographical error.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And that's why in my question earlier to you, I suggested, it was 80 to 85 per cent were people who were refugees or displaced persons, as the UNMO report reflects on the 8th of July 1995. Would that sound about accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And isn't it true, sir, that the 80 to 85 per cent of the people, not being from the enclave in Srebrenica, had no willingness to continue remain in that enclave for any period of time? Isn't that what you observed, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You didn't observe that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't observe that they didn't want to stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You observed that they wanted to stay there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as they were concerned and according to what we were seeing and getting from them is that they wanted to continue living inside the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ostojic. You have -- we need to finish as soon as possible, because I don't want to create problems for the interpreters and technicians, et cetera, so try to limit yourself as much as you can, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And happy new year.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Happy new year to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think it's going to get happier soon for you, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe tomorrow, when I go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified that you tried to inspect the Dutch-Bat Bravo Company compound in Srebrenica because you had received a report that it had been shelled. Do you recall that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall the precise source of that report or information?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That shelling, we had been told by -- by Emir. Emir is the one who told us that it had been shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you refer to the B Company compound being cratered, what are you referring to specifically, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm referring to is that there were shells that landed, that hit that particular place, and my main point is that from the BSA, they shelled that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you were shown and asked questions based upon the statement of Hasan Nuhanovic, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to just turn your attention to a couple of portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This is 1D451.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, to save time, sir, you -- do you recall testifying about a series of sitreps which you authored on the 8th, one of which my friend just showed, and on the 9th of July, which you transmitted from Srebrenica? Do you remember that, sir? Do you remember those reports?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about whether you were in fact in Srebrenica on the 8th of July. I just want to ask you: Do you have any reason to doubt the accuracy of those reports or your recollection about the date on which those reports were written and issued?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn your attention to page 2, the second page of Mr. Nuhanovic's statement, and particularly if we could look at the paragraph that begins: "On 10 July ..." "On 10 July, my colleague Emir Suljagic, who evacuated with the UNMOs on 8 July to the Dutch-Bat compound, returned to the PTT building alone. He had walked six kilometres and brought with him a military map and a Motorola radio. He said the UNMOs gave him the radio and map since he voluntarily wanted to come back to Srebrenica in order to report what was happening in the town. "We used the map to determine the coordinates of the BSA positions and impact points of the shelling. We radioed the information to the UNMOs." My question, Colonel, is: Other than the date of 8 July, which Mr. Hasan Nuhanovic has obviously recalled your withdrawal from Srebrenica, how does this passage comport with your recollection of these events?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the date, 8th July, is not when we left Srebrenica. We left Srebrenica on 9th of July. Secondly, we never gave -- we never got any reports from Hasan at all. The reports we got from one of the -- I mean, we got reports from Emir Suljagic. That is the one who gave us reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall learning at any time that Mr. Hasan Nuhanovic was spending time with Emir in the process of gathering this information? If you don't, that's fine. If you do, please let us know whether you -- whether you recall such information?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all, we never got to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn your attention to page 4. Specifically, in the middle of the paragraph that begins: "In the morning, around 0600 hours ..." This is describing events on the 11th of July: "The parking lot of the Bravo Company was crowded with people. Two shells landed in the center of the compound. The explosions were very strong. I saw five or six people laying on the ground in blood. Later, I saw the Dutch doctors trying to operate a boy. I saw a woman die at the entrance of the bunker. People panicked, screamed, and yelled at the Dutch for help." Sir, how does this portion of Mr. Hasan Nuhanovic's statement comport, if at all, with whatever the report was that you received from Emir regarding the shelling of the Bravo Company compound which you investigated on the 13th of July, when you returned to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This compares favorably, at least it's a bit of what we were told by Emir concerning the -- the shelling of that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may, I'd like to take a look at 5D3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, you were shown this document by, I believe, more than one of my friends during their cross-examination. To keep it short, it was authored by Ramiz Becirovic and describes and takes credit for several acts of sabotage by the ABiH, which resulted in significant casualties to Serbs. Do you recall that -- those questions on cross-examination, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may look at page 2 of this document, specifically paragraph 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: About midway through this paragraph, Colonel, it describes, as opposed to a couple of unsuccessful infiltrations attempted by the VRS, Mr. Becirovic describes a 24 June 1995 infiltration through a mine corridor from the Sase lead mine. Would you please just read that portion to yourself, and I want to ask you a couple questions about it.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Becirovic does not take credit for this act in this document, sir. I want to ask you: You were asked some questions about an attack from outside the enclave, inside the enclave, which resulted in some -- a death and some injuries on the 24th of June, and I believe my friend Madame Fauveau showed you an UNPROFOR report concerning that attack. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Based on a review of this paragraph, can you tell us whether or not your recollection is that this attack described herein, which Mr. Becirovic attributes to the BSA, is the same incident which you investigated and which was the subject matter of Madame Fauveau's questions on the Dutch-Bat report?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is the one, as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to ask you a couple of brief questions about this debrief that was conducted 24 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may be shown 1D470, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Paragraph 1 states that: "There were no trained debriefers present and the meeting was held in an informal atmosphere." Colonel, were you aware that the person who was interviewing you was not a trained debriefer?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we knew he was not a trained one.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 3, in the middle, it states that: "Where possible, the exact wording has been maintained, although it has been 'translated' from direct speech of a conversational nature in a situation where English was not the mother tongue." Does that comport with your recollection, sir, or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does. It does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 1, it notes that the debrief occurred from 0945 to 1130 hours. How would you describe the thoroughness of this debrief, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this debrief was very basic, very basic, in that it did not carry out everything. Not everything was asked, not everything was given, and it was sort of ad hoc. It's like they just wanted to finish with us and we go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you have your sitreps with you during this debrief, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And until today, have you ever seen this document before, sir, or been given at that opportunity to review it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the first time I'm seeing this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And while we're on the topic of interviews and reports, sir, my friend spent a great deal of time recounting to you the assessments of others about your performance during the events of the attack on the Srebrenica enclave. I want to turn your attention to a couple of sections which my friend didn't recite to you and ask you to respond in the same manner that you were asked to respond --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- to the attacks on your performance and courage. Page 4 of this document reads: "The one UNMO who appears to have been most active in those days after the fall was the Kenyan major, J. Kingori. He could, in fact, be seen in the film images made on July 12th after the entry of the Serb troops and Mladic. He was also the one who asked them why the men were being separated. "At Franken's request, he watched the white house on July 13th to check whether the number of men who were led in corresponded with the number who came out. And as Dutch-Bat soldier Kerman wrote in his diary, Kingori also protected continually against the brutal manner in which people were packed together in the buses." How does this passage comport, sir, with your recollection of these events?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that is the most accurate description of what we did and what I personally did in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we turn to page 7 of the document, there's another passage which my friend failed to cite to you; and that is: "The things that Kingori now says that he has seen appear to have been confirmed by other sources."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, other than your sitreps and the notebook which you recently reviewed, and the documents that you and I reviewed during proofing which I've enumerated for my friends, what is the basis for your testimony, for your recollection in court today?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm using what I know, what I did when I was there, what I saw, what we discussed, and also what we sent to the UNMO headquarters. This is a pure truth, as far as I can recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, one last question, sir. Do you recall where the former OP Echo was located in the enclave; to the north, south, east, or west, sir? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a difficult one. OP Echo, I really cannot -- I think it was to the -- to the west, to the -- yeah, to the west, I think. I'm not very sure, but I think it's to the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall what you told the OTP in 1997 about any BSA complaints about the Muslims' military activity within the enclave? Do you recall precisely what you told the investigator at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't -- I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right. One last document, if we may, 1D351, please. And if we may turn to page 4 of the English. There we go, and we'll be focusing on the large paragraph about halfway down the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It begins: "At one occasion ...," and in the paragraph you discuss the dinner meeting you had with Colonel Vukovic. I just want to read to you what this witness statement says: "During all these meetings, on some occasions the BSA complained about BiH strikes on the east and southeast of the enclave. During the four months of my stay, I do not remember having ever heard any complaint of the BSA about the fact that Serb civilians had been killed or injured by the Muslims from the enclave." Sir, did you make this statement to the investigators in 1997?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is it accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is accurate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We haven't got questions from the Bench, which means your testimony ends here. Colonel, I thank you for having come over to give -- to continue and finish your testimony, and on behalf of everyone I wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With your indulgence, shall we leave the exhibits for Monday. And the reason is I am getting concerned about the length of time that we have kept the interpreters, in particular, here. So thank you, Colonel. You may leave the courtroom. But before we adjourn, again I wish that also what I'm going to say be communicated to the Registrar and the head of the CNSS. You've been extremely forthcoming and cooperative, all of you, interpreters, technicians, reporters, and of course last but not least certainly counsel, and the accused themselves, and the security guards. We've kept you here for a long time, so I thank you all, and we appreciate all you have done. We also wish you a nice weekend. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 14th day of January, 2008. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
